lessons.tldr: A subquery is a query nested inside another: a **scalar** subquery yields one value, while `IN`, `EXISTS`, `ANY` and `ALL` turn a whole row set into a true, false or NULL test. They let you ask "is there a matching row?" directly, and the planner rewrites most of them into semi- and anti-joins, except `NOT IN`, whose NULL rules make it both slower and a classic source of empty results.

visualizer.title: NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS, one row at a time
visualizer.interaction: Pick an operator and step through the customers. Each comparison is shown in three-valued logic. Start with **NOT IN** and the NULL present, then flip to **NOT EXISTS**.

presets.label: The NOT IN trap
presets.lookFor: 0 vs 1,713. One refund row with a NULL `customer_id` makes every NOT IN test NULL. Filtering the NULLs out, or using NOT EXISTS, gives the right answer.

presets.label: Three-valued truth table
presets.lookFor: NULL when nothing matches and a NULL is present; true or false when a match decides it. Against an empty set, IN and ANY are false and ALL is true, even for a NULL left side. EXISTS is true for a row of NULLs.

presets.label: Plans: semi, anti, SubPlan
presets.lookFor: IN becomes a **Semi Join**, NOT EXISTS an **Anti Join**. NOT IN stays a Filter with a hashed SubPlan, which the planner cannot reorder.

presets.label: Scalar subqueries
presets.lookFor: Ava gets NULL (no rows, not 0). A scalar subquery that returns 2+ rows fails with SQLSTATE `21000` only when it runs, so it can pass tests on small data.

presets.label: ANY / ALL with arrays
presets.lookFor: `= ANY(array)` is the parameter-friendly form of IN: one bind parameter instead of a list. `>= ALL` finds the rows that are at least every value.

presets.label: ANY / ALL are min / max in disguise
presets.lookFor: Managers earn 55,000 to 60,000. `> ALL` means above the **highest** (only Bob). `> ANY` means above the **lowest** (Bob, Liam, Jack). `= ANY` is IN (Charlie). `< ALL` is below the lowest (8 people), `< ANY` below the highest (11). `SOME` is a synonym for ANY.

presets.label: Correlated subquery vs window
presets.lookFor: The first plan shows `SubPlan 1` with `loops=287`, one per joined refund: the inner join and average run again for every row. The window version joins once, sorts once and computes every country average in one **WindowAgg**. Both return the same 143 rows.

presets.label: Subquery in FROM
presets.lookFor: A derived table: aggregate per customer first, then average per country. The planner may flatten simple FROM subqueries into the outer query.

production.title: A suppression list that suppressed everyone
production.problem: One day the campaign sent zero emails. A new import path had written a single unsubscribe row with `customer_id` NULL (the address could not be linked). From then on every `NOT IN` test was NULL, and the query returned nothing. No error and no warning.
production.outcome: Correct results whatever the list contains. The plan changes from a filter with a hashed SubPlan to a Hash Anti Join, which the planner can reorder and which does not degrade to a per-row SubPlan when the list outgrows `work_mem`. With 2,000 customers and one NULL row in the list, the old query returns 0 rows and the new one 1,713.

pitfalls.title: NOT IN with a nullable column
pitfalls.fix: Use `NOT EXISTS`, or add `WHERE col IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery, and declare the column NOT NULL if NULL has no meaning.

pitfalls.title: Scalar subquery returning several rows
pitfalls.fix: Make the subquery provably single-row (aggregate, `LIMIT 1` with an `ORDER BY`, or a unique key in the WHERE), or turn it into a join or LATERAL.

pitfalls.title: Correlated subquery in the select list on a big table
pitfalls.fix: Aggregate once and join (`LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, sum(amount) … GROUP BY 1)`), use a window function (`avg(x) OVER (PARTITION BY key)`), or index the correlation column. Check `loops=` in EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

pitfalls.title: Side effects inside EXISTS
pitfalls.fix: Keep subqueries side-effect free. Do writes in data-modifying CTEs or separate statements.

keyPointers: `EXISTS` is true if at least one row comes back and is **never NULL**; the select list inside it does not matter.
`IN` = `= ANY`, `NOT IN` = `<> ALL`. With a NULL in the list and no match, both give **NULL**.
Empty subquery: `IN`/`ANY` → false, `NOT IN`/`ALL` → true.
A scalar subquery with 0 rows is NULL; with 2+ rows it is an **error**.
IN/EXISTS plan as **semi-joins**, NOT EXISTS as an **anti-join**; NOT IN stays a SubPlan filter.

lessons.title: CTEs: inlined vs MATERIALIZED
lessons.tldr: A **common table expression** (`WITH name AS (…)`) names a subquery for one statement, and since PostgreSQL 12 the planner **inlines** it when it is referenced once and has no side effects, otherwise it **materializes** it once. CTEs exist to make complex queries readable and to chain data-modifying steps in one statement, and the `MATERIALIZED` / `NOT MATERIALIZED` keywords let you decide when the planner may see through them.

visualizer.title: One CTE, five plans
visualizer.interaction: Step through the same CTE planned five ways, then a data-modifying CTE. Watch rows read and shared buffers per plan: the same 20,000-row table, five very different amounts of work.

presets.label: Inlined (default)
presets.lookFor: No CTE node at all: the plan is a Bitmap Index Scan, exactly as if you wrote `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42`.

presets.label: MATERIALIZED fence
presets.lookFor: A `CTE c` subplan scans all 20,000 rows into a tuplestore (`Storage: Memory`), then `CTE Scan` filters. Shared hits go from about 42 to 128.

presets.label: Two references
presets.lookFor: Default: CTE Scan twice over a materialized copy (128 buffers). NOT MATERIALIZED: a Nested Loop of two primary-key Index Scans (6 buffers).

presets.label: When materializing wins
presets.lookFor: The expensive aggregate runs **once** (one HashAggregate over 20,000 rows) and both references read the 500-row result. Inlining would aggregate twice.

presets.label: Same snapshot
presets.lookFor: Inside the statement the table still shows 1.99, RETURNING shows 3.98, and the next statement sees 3.98. Sub-statements cannot see each other's writes.

presets.label: Move rows atomically
presets.lookFor: DELETE and INSERT commit together or not at all. Seven days of orders move: 468 rows, leaving 19,532.

presets.label: Parent and children in one statement
presets.lookFor: The generated `invoice_id` flows from one INSERT to the next through RETURNING, never back to the client. The foreign keys are checked at the end of the statement, so the child rows may reference a parent inserted in a sibling CTE. If any part fails, nothing is written.

production.title: Removing CTE fences from a multi-tenant dashboard
production.problem: On PostgreSQL 11 every CTE was an optimization fence. Each request scanned and materialized all tenants' events, then threw away 99% of them. Someone had also added `MATERIALIZED` everywhere "for safety" while preparing the upgrade, which kept the old behaviour.
production.outcome: At 20,000 rows the gap is already 42 shared buffers inlined vs 128 materialized for one customer. The materialized cost grows with the whole table while the inlined cost grows only with one tenant's rows, so the saving grows with the number of tenants in the table.

pitfalls.title: Using a CTE as a "temporary table" for speed
pitfalls.fix: Decide with EXPLAIN. If you need computed-once semantics for an expensive or volatile expression, write `AS MATERIALIZED` explicitly.

pitfalls.title: A fence left behind by an old query
pitfalls.fix: Use `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` (if duplicated work is cheap), move the filter inside the CTE, or remove the volatile call.

pitfalls.title: Reading your own writes inside one statement
pitfalls.fix: Pass data along with `RETURNING` and select from the CTE name, not from the table. Never modify the same row in two sub-statements: which change wins is unspecified.

pitfalls.title: ORDER BY inside the CTE
pitfalls.fix: Sort in the outer query. Keep ORDER BY inside a CTE only where it feeds `LIMIT` or an order-sensitive step in that same CTE.

keyPointers: Default: a side-effect-free, non-recursive CTE referenced **once** is **inlined**; referenced 2+ times it is **materialized** once.
`AS MATERIALIZED` forces a fence; `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` forces inlining of every reference.
Volatile functions, data-modifying statements and recursion always materialize.
Data-modifying CTEs run once, to completion, on the **same snapshot**; use RETURNING to pass rows on.
In EXPLAIN, a `CTE Scan` node means materialized; no CTE node means inlined.

lessons.title: Recursive CTEs
lessons.tldr: A `WITH RECURSIVE` query is a non-recursive term `UNION [ALL]` a recursive term, evaluated **iteratively**: each pass feeds only the previous pass's new rows (the **working table**) back into the recursive term until no new rows appear. It is how SQL walks trees and graphs of unknown depth (org charts, bills of materials, routes) in one statement, and the `CYCLE` and `SEARCH` clauses make loops and ordering explicit.

visualizer.title: Working table, intermediate table, result
visualizer.interaction: Step through the algorithm one pass at a time. Start with the org chart, then switch to the graph and compare **UNION ALL** (runs forever), **UNION** and the **CYCLE** clause.

presets.label: Everyone under Raj
presets.lookFor: 6 rows in four passes: Raj (depth 0), Omar and Ivy, Zoe and Kai, then Noor. The fifth pass finds nobody and the loop stops.

presets.label: Self-join: one level per join
presets.lookFor: Two joins find Omar, Ivy, Zoe and Kai, and miss Noor on level 3. The recursive version adds 1, 2, 2, 1 rows per pass and stops when a pass adds nothing. In the plan, **Recursive Union** runs the recursive term against a **WorkTable Scan**: the previous pass's rows only.

presets.label: Path to the top
presets.lookFor: Walking **upwards** is the same algorithm with the join reversed: Noor → Zoe → Omar → Raj → Maya.

presets.label: SEARCH DEPTH / BREADTH FIRST
presets.lookFor: `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST` adds an `ord` column (the path of ids) to sort by, giving an indented outline. Use `SEARCH BREADTH FIRST` to order level by level. Never rely on the natural output order.

presets.label: CYCLE detection
presets.lookFor: 5 rows. The row that returns to A has `is_cycle = true` and is not expanded. Without the CYCLE clause this query never terminates.

presets.label: UNION vs UNION ALL
presets.lookFor: With only `node`, UNION discards the repeat of A and stops after 4 rows. Add `hops` and no row ever repeats, so UNION no longer protects you. The LIMIT works only because the outer query stops fetching.

presets.label: A calendar without gaps
presets.lookFor: A counter with a stop condition in WHERE. For plain series, `generate_series` is simpler and faster.

production.title: Expanding a bill of materials for a manufacturer
production.problem: The application walked the tree with one query per level. A deep product took 9 round trips, and a data-entry error that made an assembly contain itself sent the loop spinning until the request timed out.
production.outcome: One round trip whatever the depth, and a cyclic definition terminates with `is_cycle = true` rows that a check can alert on. Add an index on `parts(assembly_id)`: the recursive term joins the working table to it once per level.

pitfalls.title: Infinite recursion on cyclic data
pitfalls.fix: Add `CYCLE col SET is_cycle USING path`, or a depth limit in the recursive term (`WHERE depth < 20`). Do not rely on a LIMIT in the outer query: it stops working as soon as the outer query sorts or joins.

pitfalls.title: Relying on breadth-first output order
pitfalls.fix: Add `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY id SET ord` (or BREADTH FIRST) and `ORDER BY ord` in the outer query.

pitfalls.title: Expecting UNION to stop a loop
pitfalls.fix: Track visited nodes explicitly with `CYCLE`, or keep the CTE's columns to the node key only when that is all you need.

pitfalls.title: Anchor and recursive term with columns in a different order
pitfalls.fix: Name the CTE columns once (`WITH RECURSIVE sub(id, manager_id) AS …`) and list them in the same order in both terms.

keyPointers: Shape: **non-recursive term** `UNION [ALL]` **recursive term**; only the recursive term may reference the CTE, once.
Each pass reads only the **working table** (last pass's new rows); recursion ends when a pass produces nothing.
UNION drops rows that duplicate **any earlier row**; UNION ALL keeps everything.
`CYCLE col SET is_cycle USING path` stops loops; `SEARCH DEPTH|BREADTH FIRST BY col SET ord` gives a sortable order.
Recursive CTEs are always materialized; data-modifying statements cannot be recursive.

lessons.title: Window functions and frames
lessons.tldr: A **window function** computes a value for every row from a set of related rows (its partition, and for aggregates and value functions a **frame** inside it), without collapsing rows the way GROUP BY does. It answers "compared with its neighbours" questions in one pass: rankings, running totals, moving averages, previous-row deltas and top-N per group, where a self-join or correlated subquery would be slower and harder to read.

visualizer.title: The window frame explorer
visualizer.interaction: Click a row to make it current, then change mode, bounds, offset and EXCLUDE. Start with **Default frame** on Sony VAIO (a three-way tie at 700), then compare **Running total**.

presets.label: Rows stay, unlike GROUP BY
presets.lookFor: GROUP BY returns 3 rows. The window version returns all 11, each with its group's average attached (Laptop 850, Smartphone 500, Tablet 350).

presets.label: Ranking with ties
presets.lookFor: Lenovo and Sony tie at 700: row_number 1,2 (arbitrary order), rank 1,1,3,4 (gap), dense_rank 1,1,2,3 (no gap). `percent_rank` = (rank − 1) / (rows − 1), so the first row is always 0. `cume_dist` = rows up to the last peer / rows: 0.5 for both 700s. `ntile(3)` over 4 rows makes buckets of 2, 1, 1: bigger buckets come first.

presets.label: The default frame trap
presets.lookFor: All three 700 rows show `range_default` = 3550 (peers share the frame end), while `rows_running` differs across them, in an order PostgreSQL does not guarantee. `last_default` is just the current row's last peer; `last_whole` is HP Elite everywhere.

presets.label: Cheapest per group
presets.lookFor: Window functions run after WHERE, so filtering on the rank needs a subquery. dense_rank keeps **both** 700s in Laptop; row_number would silently pick one.

presets.label: LAG: year over year
presets.lookFor: The first year of each group has no previous row, so `lag` returns NULL (pass a third argument for a default). `lag` and `lead` ignore the frame. They look at the previous **row**, not the previous year: if 2019 were missing, 2020 would be compared with 2018. And with `ORDER BY year DESC`, `lag` returns the following year.

presets.label: Percent of total in one pass
presets.lookFor: `sum(…) OVER ()` puts the grand total (20.8) on every row, so no CROSS JOIN to a total subquery is needed. Changing only the window to `PARTITION BY band` switches the denominator to the band total: Stills is 30.3% of all earnings but 48.5% of CSNY. The second query works because windows run **after** GROUP BY: CSNY 62.5%, PPM 37.5%.

presets.label: Fill gaps: last known value
presets.lookFor: `count(temperature)` skips NULLs, so the running count only rises on a real reading: every NULL row inherits the group of the last reading. `first_value` within that group carries 22.50 forward twice and 23.10 once. A plain `lag` is no fix: after two NULLs in a row it returns NULL.

presets.label: Moving window: ROWS vs RANGE
presets.lookFor: Compare with the explorer's presets: ROWS counts rows, RANGE compares price values, GROUPS counts distinct prices.

production.title: Deduplicating a change-data feed: latest row per key
production.problem: The first query used a correlated subquery `WHERE changed_at = (SELECT max(changed_at) … WHERE customer_id = c.customer_id)`. It ran one subquery per row, and returned two rows when two changes shared a timestamp.
production.outcome: One scan and one sort instead of one subquery per row, and a deterministic answer when timestamps tie, thanks to the `change_id` tie-breaker. An index on `(customer_id, changed_at DESC, change_id DESC)` can provide the order and skip the sort.

pitfalls.title: last_value returns the current row
pitfalls.fix: Add `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`, or use `first_value(…)` with the ORDER BY reversed.

pitfalls.title: Running totals that jump on ties
pitfalls.fix: Use `ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING` and add a unique tie-breaker to the ORDER BY (`ORDER BY booked_at, id`) so the order is deterministic.

pitfalls.title: Filtering on a window function in WHERE
pitfalls.fix: Compute the window function in a subquery or CTE, then filter in the outer query.

pitfalls.title: A ROWS window treated as a time window
pitfalls.fix: Use `RANGE BETWEEN interval '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` on a date column, or fill the gaps with `generate_series` first.

pitfalls.title: DISTINCT does not deduplicate a row_number()
pitfalls.fix: Deduplicate first, then number: `SELECT price, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY price) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT price FROM products) p` (8 rows instead of 11). Or use `dense_rank()`, which gives equal values the same number.

pitfalls.title: Top-N with LIMIT on a tie
pitfalls.fix: Add a unique tie-breaker (`ORDER BY price DESC, product_id`), or include every tie with `FETCH FIRST 4 ROWS WITH TIES` (6 rows here) or `rank() <= 4`.

keyPointers: Window functions run **after** WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING and never collapse rows.
**Peers** are rows equal under the window ORDER BY; rank functions give peers the same value.
Default frame with ORDER BY: `RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING` to the current row's **last peer**; without ORDER BY: the whole partition.
`ROWS` counts rows, `RANGE` compares values (one ORDER BY column for offsets), `GROUPS` counts peer groups; `EXCLUDE` trims the result.
Frames matter for aggregates and `first_value`/`last_value`/`nth_value`, not for `row_number`, `rank`, `lag` or `lead`.

lessons.title: LATERAL joins
lessons.tldr: A `LATERAL` subquery in FROM may reference columns of the FROM items to its left, so it is evaluated **once per outer row**, like the body of a for-each loop. It exists for questions a plain join cannot express, such as "the latest N rows for each parent" or "expand this row's array", and with the right index it is often the fastest top-N-per-group plan.

visualizer.title: LATERAL as a for-each loop
visualizer.interaction: Step through the outer rows and watch the subquery re-run with each `a.id`. Compare **CROSS JOIN LATERAL** (5 rows) with **LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true** (6 rows), and try the plain JOIN to see the error.

presets.label: Without LATERAL: an error
presets.lookFor: `42P01: invalid reference to FROM-clause entry for table "a"`. A plain FROM subquery cannot see its neighbours.

presets.label: Latest 2 per account
presets.lookFor: 5 rows. Umbrella has no purchases, so CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops it.

presets.label: Keep empty parents
presets.lookFor: 6 rows: Umbrella appears with NULLs. `ON true` is required syntax for LEFT JOIN; the real condition lives inside the subquery.

presets.label: loops=4 and the index
presets.lookFor: A **Nested Loop** whose inner side shows `loops=4`. With the index the inner side is an Index Scan that reads at most 2 entries per account, no sort.

presets.label: Functions are implicitly lateral
presets.lookFor: A set-returning function in FROM may always reference earlier items, with or without the keyword. `WITH ORDINALITY` adds a bigint position column. Initech has no tags: dropped by the comma form, kept by LEFT JOIN.

presets.label: Split a CSV column (and the text trap)
presets.lookFor: `string_to_array` returns `text[]`, so the first query compares **strings**: North's minimum is '-1' (true value −16) and West's maximum is '9' (true 16). Casting to `int[]` fixes it. The last query numbers each reading with `WITH ORDINALITY` and keeps the top one per station: hour 8 at West (16°), hour 7 at South (33°).

presets.label: LATERAL vs a window function
presets.lookFor: Same 5 rows. The window version numbers **every** purchase and then filters; LATERAL + LIMIT with an index reads only the rows it returns. With few parents and many children per parent, LATERAL wins.

production.title: An activity feed: latest 3 events per followed user
production.problem: The original query ranked all posts of all followed accounts with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY author_id ORDER BY created_at DESC)` and then filtered `rn <= 3`. For a user following prolific accounts it sorted hundreds of thousands of rows to return 600.
production.outcome: The plan becomes a Nested Loop with an Index Scan inside, `loops` = number of followed accounts, and at most 3 index entries read per loop: about 600 rows touched instead of every post of those authors.

pitfalls.title: CROSS JOIN LATERAL silently drops parents
pitfalls.fix: Use `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (…) p ON true` to keep every outer row, NULL-extended.

pitfalls.title: LATERAL without a supporting index
pitfalls.fix: Create an index on `(correlation_column, sort_column DESC)` so each loop is a short index scan, and check `loops=` in EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

pitfalls.title: Referencing the right side from a RIGHT/FULL join
pitfalls.fix: Rewrite with the LATERAL item on the right side of an inner or LEFT join.

pitfalls.title: Max-then-join-back for "latest per group"
pitfalls.fix: Use LATERAL with `ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1`, or `DISTINCT ON (account_id) … ORDER BY account_id, created_at DESC, id DESC`. Both return exactly one row per key, with a deterministic tie-breaker.

keyPointers: `LATERAL` lets a FROM subquery reference columns of FROM items **to its left**; it runs once per outer row.
Set-returning functions in FROM are **implicitly lateral**; the keyword is optional there.
CROSS JOIN / comma LATERAL drops rows with an empty result; `LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true` keeps them.
Top-N per group: LATERAL + `ORDER BY … LIMIT n` + index on `(key, sort DESC)` → Nested Loop with Index Scan.
`WITH ORDINALITY` numbers the rows of a function in FROM (bigint, from 1).

lessons.title: Aggregates, FILTER and GROUPING SETS
lessons.tldr: An **aggregate** folds many input rows into one value per group, and `FILTER`, ordered-set aggregates and `GROUPING SETS` / `ROLLUP` / `CUBE` control which rows feed it and which groupings are produced. Together they turn a dozen report queries (totals, subtotals, conditional counts, medians) into one pass over the data, provided you respect the NULL rules that make `count(col)` differ from `count(*)` and `sum` of nothing NULL.

visualizer.title: Grouping sets, one set at a time
visualizer.interaction: Pick ROLLUP, CUBE or your own GROUPING SETS and step through each set. Watch which input rows fold together, and how `grouping()` tells a subtotal's NULL from Baz's real NULL size.

presets.label: CUBE and grouping()
presets.lookFor: 12 rows. Two rows read `NULL, NULL`: sum 8 with g = 2 (Baz's real NULL size, grouped by size) and sum 58 with g = 3 (the grand total).

presets.label: Four queries, or one GROUPING SETS
presets.lookFor: The UNION ALL plan is an **Append** of four aggregates, each over its own Seq Scan. GROUPING SETS returns the same 12 rows from one **MixedAggregate** (one Hash Key per set, `Group Key: ()` for the total) over a single scan. `CUBE (brand, size)` is shorthand for exactly these four sets.

presets.label: ROLLUP with labels
presets.lookFor: ROLLUP gives detail rows, a subtotal per brand and a grand total. The plan is one **MixedAggregate** with a Hash Key per set: a single scan.

presets.label: count(*) vs count(col)
presets.lookFor: `count(*)` counts rows, `count(col)` skips NULLs (40 orders have no amount, so `avg` ignores them: 104.63). Dividing `sum` by `count(*)` counts those 40 rows as zeros and gives 102.54. Over zero rows `sum` is **NULL**, not 0; only count returns 0.

presets.label: FILTER: one pass, many counts
presets.lookFor: Each aggregate sees only the rows its FILTER allows, all in a single scan. Clearer than `sum(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`, and it works with any aggregate: `array_agg(x) FILTER (…)` skips rows, while the CASE trick would collect NULLs. FILTER is standard SQL, not a PostgreSQL extension.

presets.label: Median and mode
presets.lookFor: Ordered-set aggregates sort their input. `percentile_cont` interpolates between the two middle values; `percentile_disc` returns an actual input value. There is no separate `median()`: `percentile_cont(0.5)` is the median.

presets.label: WHERE vs HAVING
presets.lookFor: Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE (`42803`): WHERE filters input rows, HAVING filters groups after aggregation. HAVING cannot use the output alias `total` either (`42703`), because the SELECT list is computed after HAVING. Logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. ORDER BY can use output names, and so can GROUP BY as a PostgreSQL extension; WHERE and HAVING cannot.

presets.label: DISTINCT ON: first row per key
presets.lookFor: One row per region: the first after sorting, here the largest order. The DISTINCT ON expressions must lead the ORDER BY; add a tie-breaker (`id`) for a deterministic pick.

production.title: A finance dashboard: from 9 queries to 1
production.problem: It ran 9 separate queries (one per breakdown and metric), each scanning the orders table, and the page took seconds. Subtotal rows were found with `WHERE month IS NULL`, which also caught orders whose month column was legitimately NULL.
production.outcome: One scan feeding one MixedAggregate instead of nine scans. For 4 regions and 2 months that is 4 × 2 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 rows. Subtotal rows are identified by `level`, so a real NULL can never be mistaken for a total.

pitfalls.title: sum() of no rows is NULL
pitfalls.fix: Wrap it: `coalesce(sum(amount), 0)`. For arrays, `coalesce(array_agg(x), '{}')`. The same applies to FILTER: a month with no matching rows gives `sum(x) FILTER (…)` = NULL, so a CASE or FILTER rewrite of a report that used to print 0 needs the COALESCE back.

pitfalls.title: count(col) where count(*) was meant
pitfalls.fix: Use `count(*)` to count rows; use `count(col)` only when "rows with a value" is what you mean.

pitfalls.title: Telling subtotals apart with IS NULL
pitfalls.fix: Use `grouping(col)`: 1 means the NULL is a subtotal placeholder, 0 means it is data.

pitfalls.title: Order-sensitive aggregates without ORDER BY
pitfalls.fix: Put the order inside the call: `string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name)`, `array_agg(x ORDER BY ts)`.

pitfalls.title: BETWEEN on a timestamp drops the last day
pitfalls.fix: Use a half-open range: `created_at >= '2026-10-01' AND created_at < '2026-11-01'`. It is exact for dates and timestamps, never double-counts, and an index can use it.

pitfalls.title: Integer division in ratios
pitfalls.fix: Make one operand numeric first (`100.0 * count(*) FILTER (…) / count(*)`) and guard the denominator with `NULLIF(count(*), 0)`, which turns 0 into NULL so the ratio is NULL instead of an error.

keyPointers: `count(*)` counts rows; `count(col)` counts non-NULL values; every other aggregate returns **NULL** on no rows.
`agg(...) FILTER (WHERE ...)` restricts one aggregate's input; WHERE restricts all rows; HAVING filters groups.
`ROLLUP (a, b)` = (a,b), (a), (); `CUBE (a, b)` = all 4 subsets; all sets run in one scan.
`grouping(a, b)` is a bitmask: bit = 1 when that column is **not** grouped in the current row's set.
Ordered-set aggregates: `percentile_cont` interpolates, `percentile_disc` picks a value, `mode()` returns the most frequent.

modules.title: Query Planner, Optimizer & Indexing
modules.summary: From SQL text to a plan tree: costs, statistics, every index access method, and reading EXPLAIN like a pro.

lessons.title: From SQL text to rows: parse, analyze, rewrite, plan, execute
lessons.tldr: Every statement passes through five stages: a **parser** that knows only grammar, **analysis** that resolves names against the catalogs, a **rewriter** that expands views and rules, a **planner** that costs alternative paths, and an **executor** that pulls rows up a plan tree. Splitting the work this way lets PostgreSQL parse transaction commands without a transaction, reuse analyzed statements through **PREPARE**, and pick among many equivalent plans by estimated cost.

visualizer.title: Follow one query through the backend
visualizer.interaction: Step through a join against a view, from characters to tokens, trees, costed paths and finally rows pulled up the plan. Switch modes to watch the plan cache decide between custom and generic plans.

presets.label: The view is a rule
presets.lookFor: A view is stored as a `_RETURN` rule (`ev_type` 1 = SELECT). The rewriter pastes this definition into every query that names the view.

presets.label: The view disappears
presets.lookFor: The plan scans `public.orders` directly with the view's `amount > 900` filter. After rewriting and subquery pull-up, `big_orders` no longer exists.

presets.label: Three join paths
presets.lookFor: Disabling the winner reveals the runner-up paths the planner costed: merge join (about 2788), then nested loop with Memoize (about 3528). The hash join (about 2022) won.

presets.label: Demand-pull counts
presets.lookFor: Each node reports the rows it handed to its parent: customers 1250 (3750 removed), orders 9700 (90300 removed), join 2425.

presets.label: Subqueries become joins
presets.lookFor: The planner rewrites EXISTS into a join: here a Hash Join over the de-duplicated customer ids. NOT EXISTS becomes a **Hash Right Anti Join** estimated at 3974 rows. NOT IN cannot become an anti join, because one NULL in the subquery would make every row unknown. It stays a `hashed SubPlan` filter, with a blind 2500-row guess.

presets.label: CTE: inlined or materialized
presets.lookFor: A plain CTE used once is **inlined**: the outer filter joins it, and a BitmapAnd of two indexes finds 1 row (cost about 21). `MATERIALIZED` computes all 1027 pending rows first, then filters a `CTE Scan` (cost about 155).

presets.label: Custom → generic
presets.lookFor: Five custom plans, then the generic plan wins: `generic_plans = 1`. EXPLAIN shows `customer_id = $1`, a plan built without knowing the value.

presets.label: Skew keeps it custom
presets.lookFor: The generic plan assumes 50000 matching rows and costs far more than the custom plans, so `generic_plans` stays 0.

production.title: A prepared statement that turned slow on the sixth call
production.problem: Latency for small tenants jumped after a connection had served a few requests. The first five executions got custom plans. Then the cached **generic plan** won the cost comparison, and it was tuned for an average tenant, so it walked the big tenant's part of the index for everyone.
production.outcome: Every execution is planned with the real tenant id, so small tenants get an index scan on their own rows again. The cost is one planning pass per call, which `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` reports as Planning Time (about 0.1 to 0.9 ms in the playground).

pitfalls.title: Generic plans on skewed parameters
pitfalls.fix: Check `generic_plans` in `pg_prepared_statements` and compare `EXPLAIN EXECUTE` with `EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN)`. Set `plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan` for that workload.

pitfalls.title: Expecting a view to be cached
pitfalls.fix: Use a **materialized view** (refreshed explicitly) or a summary table when you need the result stored.

pitfalls.title: Big joins switch to GEQO
pitfalls.fix: Reduce the join count (pre-aggregate, split the query), or write joins in a good order and set `join_collapse_limit = 1` for that query. `geqo_seed` makes the choice repeatable.

pitfalls.title: Using a CTE as an optimization fence, or as a cache
pitfalls.fix: Write `AS MATERIALIZED` when you really want compute-once or a fence, and `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` to allow inlining of a CTE that is referenced several times. Check the plan for a `CTE Scan` node.

pitfalls.title: NOT IN over a nullable subquery
pitfalls.fix: Write `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t WHERE t.ref = x.id)`. It is NULL-safe and becomes an Anti Join.

keyPointers: Stages: **parser** (grammar only, no catalogs) → **analysis** (names, types, operators) → **rewriter** (views, rules) → **planner** (paths, costs) → **executor**.
The rewriter turns query trees into query trees. A view is a `_RETURN` rule expanded like a macro, then usually flattened into the outer query.
The planner costs **paths** for each relation, then join pairs, keeping the cheapest. Above `geqo_threshold` = 12 FROM items it switches to GEQO.
The executor is **demand-pull**: each node returns one row per call, or NULL when done. Hash and Sort must drain their input first.
**PREPARE** caches the analyzed tree. Five custom plans, then a generic plan if its cost is not much higher (`plan_cache_mode`).

lessons.title: The cost model
lessons.tldr: The planner prices every candidate plan in abstract **cost units**, where reading one page sequentially costs `seq_page_cost` = 1.0 and every random page, row, index entry and operator call has its own relative price. Comparing those totals is how PostgreSQL decides between a sequential scan, an index scan and a bitmap scan, so the constants (and the statistics they multiply) decide which plan you get.

visualizer.title: Where the sequential scan starts to win
visualizer.interaction: Drag the predicate wider and watch three real cost curves cross. Then make the column scattered, shrink the cache, and lower `random_page_cost` to see each factor move the crossover.

presets.label: Seq scan formula
presets.lookFor: 935 pages × 1.0 + 100000 rows × 0.01 = **1935**. Adding one filter adds 100000 × `cpu_operator_cost` 0.0025 = 250, giving **2185**.

presets.label: Cost constants
presets.lookFor: Defaults: random 4.0, tuple 0.01, index tuple 0.005, operator 0.0025. `effective_cache_size` is a hint for costing only: it allocates nothing.

presets.label: Correlation matters
presets.lookFor: Same 5% of rows. The correlated column gets a cheap Index Scan (about 193). The scattered one gets a Bitmap Heap Scan (about 1090), because those rows are spread over almost every page.

presets.label: Scattered rows, every page
presets.lookFor: `Heap Blocks: exact=934`: only 2% of the rows, but they live on 934 of the 935 pages. That is why the bitmap scan is nearly as expensive as a full scan.

presets.label: Tiny table, index ignored
presets.lookFor: 200 rows fit in **2 pages**. Reading both and testing 200 rows costs 2 + 2 + 0.5 = **4.50**. The index path costs 8.16, because it reads index pages and then a random heap page. At 20000 rows the same query switches to the Index Scan (8.30). An unused index on a tiny table is the planner working correctly.

presets.label: Startup cost and LIMIT
presets.lookFor: A Sort has a large **startup cost**: it must read everything before returning a row. The index scan under LIMIT starts at 0.29 and the Limit node charges only a fraction of the total.

presets.label: SSD pricing
presets.lookFor: At 1.1 the random heap fetches look almost as cheap as sequential ones, so the plan cost drops and index plans win over a wider range.

presets.label: enable_* only discourages
presets.lookFor: There is no index on `note`, so a seq scan is the only path and it is still used. PostgreSQL 18 marks it `Disabled: true`.

production.title: Moving a reporting database to NVMe without telling the planner
production.problem: Dashboards filtering on scattered columns kept choosing full sequential scans of large tables, even when the filter matched well under 1% of rows. The planner was still pricing every random read at four sequential reads and assumed almost nothing was cached.
production.outcome: On the playground table, at 1.1 the 1% scattered-column bitmap plan drops from cost 999 to 661, plain index scans win at 40–50% of the table, and the seq scan wins only from 70% instead of 50%. On a large table the same shift turns many seq scans into index plans. Check the slow queries with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` before and after.

pitfalls.title: Testing plans with enable_seqscan = off
pitfalls.fix: Use the flag only to see the alternative's cost. Then fix the inputs: statistics (`ANALYZE`, a higher statistics target) or cost constants. Compare `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` runs, not costs alone.

pitfalls.title: Comparing cost numbers across queries
pitfalls.fix: Rank queries by measured time and buffers (`pg_stat_statements`, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`). Use costs to understand why one plan beat another.

pitfalls.title: Leaving random_page_cost at the spinning-disk default
pitfalls.fix: Set `random_page_cost` close to `seq_page_cost` (1.1 is common for SSD) and size `effective_cache_size` honestly. Change one setting at a time and re-check key plans.

keyPointers: Unit: one sequential page = `seq_page_cost` **1.0**. Defaults: random page **4.0**, row **0.01**, index entry **0.005**, operator **0.0025**.
Seq scan = **pages × seq_page_cost + rows × cpu_tuple_cost**, plus `cpu_operator_cost` per qual per row. It does not depend on selectivity.
Index scans cost heap fetches between "sequential" and "random" depending on **correlation**. Bitmap scans read each heap page once, in physical order.
Every plan shows **startup..total** cost. LIMIT and EXISTS favour low startup cost.
`enable_*` flags only discourage a node (`Disabled: true`). `effective_cache_size` is a costing hint, not an allocation.

lessons.title: Planner statistics
lessons.tldr: `ANALYZE` samples each table and stores per-column **statistics** (null fraction, distinct count, most common values, an equal-frequency histogram and physical correlation) that the planner turns into row-count estimates. Every cost in a plan is multiplied by those estimates, so knowing how `eqsel` and `scalarltsel` read `pg_stats` (and where their independence assumption breaks) explains most bad plans.

visualizer.title: Estimate rows from a real pg_stats row
visualizer.interaction: Drag the constant and watch the MCV list and histogram produce the estimate, matched against PostgreSQL's own number and the true count. The third mode shows correlated columns and extended statistics.

presets.label: Before the first ANALYZE
presets.lookFor: Never analyzed: `reltuples = -1`, and the plan guesses **rows=8 width=240**. The width comes from the declared `varchar(50)` sizes, and the row count from a default selectivity. After ANALYZE: rows=25, width=15, and the real count is 25.

presets.label: Read pg_stats
presets.lookFor: `zone` (target 10): 10 MCVs covering 48.5% of rows and 11 histogram bounds. `id`: `n_distinct = -1` means "unique", and the histogram has 101 bounds at the default target of 100.

presets.label: Under the hood: pg_statistic
presets.lookFor: `pg_stats` is a readable view over this catalog. Each column has five slots; `stakind` says what a slot holds: **1** = most common values (frequencies in `stanumbers`), **2** = histogram bounds, **3** = correlation. A unique column has no MCV slot, so it starts with the histogram.

presets.label: Equality: MCV vs not
presets.lookFor: zone 7 is an MCV with frequency 0.2214, so the estimate is 4428. zone 99 is not, so it gets (1 − 0.48515) / 490 × 20000 = **21** rows.

presets.label: Range: MCV + histogram
presets.lookFor: MCVs 7, 3, 12 and 40 contribute 0.4753 exactly. The histogram adds one full bucket plus 9/54 of bucket 51–105, times the non-MCV share 0.515. Estimate **10686**, actual 10706.

presets.label: Independence assumption
presets.lookFor: zip determines city, but the planner multiplies their selectivities: **5** rows estimated vs 100 real, and 2000 groups vs 200.

presets.label: Extended statistics
presets.lookFor: `{"4 => 5": 1.000000}`: column 4 (zip) fully determines column 5 (city). Estimates become 100 rows and 200 groups. CREATE STATISTICS collects nothing until ANALYZE runs.

presets.label: Statistics target
presets.lookFor: With target 100 the MCV list grows to 100 entries and the histogram gets more bounds, so more values get exact frequencies instead of the uniform guess.

production.title: A nested loop over 50,000 "one row" matches
production.problem: The planner multiplied the two selectivities and estimated a handful of rows. It chose a nested loop that probed another large table once per row. The real count was tens of thousands, and the query ran for seconds.
production.outcome: In the playground's version of the same shape, the estimate goes from 5 rows to 100 (actual 100) and GROUP BY from 2000 groups to 200 (actual 200). With correct estimates the planner switches to a hash join on the real workload.

pitfalls.title: No statistics after a bulk load
pitfalls.fix: Run `ANALYZE` as the last step of every bulk load or migration, and after creating an **expression index** (its expression gets its own statistics).

pitfalls.title: Correlated columns
pitfalls.fix: Create extended statistics (`dependencies`, `ndistinct` or `mcv`) on the column group, then ANALYZE. Use `mcv` when value combinations matter or when filters are not plain equality.

pitfalls.title: n_distinct badly estimated from the sample
pitfalls.fix: Raise the target for that column, or pin the value: `ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET (n_distinct = -0.05)` (negative means a fraction of rows), then ANALYZE.

keyPointers: `pg_stats`: **null_frac**, **n_distinct** (positive count, negative fraction, −1 unique), **most_common_vals/freqs**, **histogram_bounds**, **correlation**.
`=` on an MCV uses its frequency. Otherwise **(1 − Σ mcv freqs − null_frac) / (n_distinct − #MCVs)**.
`<` sums matching MCV freqs exactly, then adds histogram buckets (linear inside a bucket) scaled by the non-MCV fraction.
ANDed predicates are **multiplied**. Correlated columns need `CREATE STATISTICS` (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv) plus ANALYZE.
`default_statistics_target` = **100** caps MCVs and histogram buckets. ANALYZE samples 300 × the largest target rows.

lessons.title: B-Tree internals: splits, high keys and right-links
lessons.tldr: PostgreSQL's default index is a **B+tree** whose pages are sibling-linked on every level, and every page except the rightmost carries a **high key**, the upper bound of the keys it may hold. Those two additions, from **Lehman & Yao**, let readers descend without locking parents: a reader that lands on a page split behind its back notices its key exceeds the high key and simply **moves right**.

visualizer.title: Grow a B-Tree, one key at a time
visualizer.interaction: Insert keys and watch descents and page splits. Then reset, switch to **random keys**, and compare page count and leaf fill. That gap is the UUIDv4 vs UUIDv7 story.

presets.label: Metapage
presets.lookFor: Block 0 is the **metapage**. `level` is the root height (0 = the root is a leaf). `allequalimage` = true means deduplication is safe.

presets.label: A leaf page
presets.lookFor: `btpo_prev`/`btpo_next` are the sibling links. **Item 1 is the high key**: it is the first key of the right sibling, not a row on this page.

presets.label: Root & downlinks
presets.lookFor: On internal pages, `ctid` holds `(child block, …)`: a downlink, not a heap row. The first item has no key and covers "minus infinity".

presets.label: v4 vs v7 vs bigint
presets.lookFor: Same row count. Random UUIDv4 keys split pages all over the index (about 23% more pages here). UUIDv7 and bigint append at the right edge and pack leaves to about 90%.

presets.label: Leaf fill %
presets.lookFor: Walks every leaf with `bt_page_stats`. Expect about 90% for sequential keys and about 70% for random ones. Random fill keeps drifting lower as the index grows.

presets.label: Index scan buffers
presets.lookFor: An equality lookup touches only a handful of buffers (metapage, root, leaf, heap page). `Index Searches: 1` (new in 18) counts descents of the tree.

production.title: Switching primary keys from UUIDv4 to UUIDv7
production.problem: Every insert landed on a **random leaf**. With the index larger than cache, most inserts first had to read a cold leaf from disk, and full leaves split down the middle, leaving pages about 65% full at scale. Checkpoints also had to write a full-page image for every scattered leaf they touched.
production.outcome: UUIDv4 needs 23% more index pages than UUIDv7 at 20k rows and 39% more at 100k rows (64.7% vs 89.8% leaf fill). In production the bigger win is locality: inserts touch one hot leaf instead of thousands of cold ones, so fewer reads and less full-page-image WAL.

pitfalls.title: Random keys on a large, write-heavy table
pitfalls.fix: Use time-ordered keys (`bigint` identity or `uuidv7()`). If a random id must be exposed externally, keep it as a secondary unique column and leave the primary key sequential.

pitfalls.title: Indexing values that are too large
pitfalls.fix: Index a hash or prefix instead: `CREATE INDEX ON docs (md5(body))` for equality lookups, a trigram GIN index for search, or a `left(col, 100)` expression index.

pitfalls.title: Bloat after mass deletes
pitfalls.fix: Run `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx;` (no long write lock), then check the size with `pg_relation_size`. For time-based purges, partition and drop whole partitions instead.

keyPointers: Block 0 is the **metapage**. The **root** can move up as the tree grows. Leaf and internal pages on each level form a **doubly-linked list**.
Every non-rightmost page stores a **high key**. If a reader's key is greater than it, the reader follows the **right-link**: that is the Lehman & Yao move-right rule.
When a page is full: try **deleting dead entries**, then **deduplicate** into posting lists, and only then **split**. Splits cascade upward, and a root split adds a level.
Appending new largest keys fills leaves to **fillfactor 90**; random keys split pages in half, leaving leaves only about 65–72% full.
Entries max out at about **1/3 page** (2704 bytes); index a hash or prefix of big values.

lessons.title: Hash indexes
lessons.tldr: A hash index stores only a **4-byte hash code** per row, grouped into **buckets** that a lookup reaches directly from the metapage, without descending a tree. That makes it compact for long keys and cheap for pure equality lookups, at the price of no ranges, no ordering, no uniqueness and no multicolumn support.

visualizer.title: Linear hashing, one bucket split at a time
visualizer.interaction: Insert keys and follow each hash code through the masks into a bucket. Watch exactly one bucket split when the fill factor is exceeded, then insert a duplicate key until it grows an overflow chain.

presets.label: Empty metapage
presets.lookFor: An empty int4 hash index already has **8 buckets** (`maxbucket` 7, `highmask` 15, `lowmask` 7), 10 pages counting the metapage and bitmap page. `ffactor` 307 is the target tuples per bucket.

presets.label: One bucket split
presets.lookFor: 2456 = 307 × 8 tuples fit. Row 2457 crosses the threshold, so `maxbucket` goes 7 → 8: exactly **one** bucket split.

presets.label: Page types
presets.lookFor: Block 0 is the **metapage**, then primary **bucket** pages, a **bitmap** page that tracks free overflow pages, and more buckets added in batches as the index grows.

presets.label: Only the hash is stored
presets.lookFor: Each item is a heap `ctid` plus a 32-bit hash code, sorted by hash within the page. The key itself is not stored, so every match is rechecked against the heap.

presets.label: Duplicates → overflow
presets.lookFor: 800 copies of one key all land in one bucket. Its primary page overflows into a chain of 2 overflow pages, and the Bitmap Index Scan reads all 3 pages of that bucket.

presets.label: Long keys: hash vs B-tree
presets.lookFor: For ~90-byte URLs the hash index is smaller than the B-tree (about 2.0 MB vs 2.4 MB) and a lookup reads about 3 buffers. For a 16-byte uuid the opposite happens: hash 1040 kB vs B-tree 632 kB at 20000 rows.

production.title: Deduplicating long URLs in a crawler
production.problem: A B-tree on `url` stored every full string, so the index was nearly as large as the table and lookups touched more pages than necessary. Very long URLs also risked the B-tree entry limit of about a third of a page.
production.outcome: In the playground, 20000 URLs of about 90 bytes give a 2.0 MB hash index against 2.4 MB for the B-tree, and a lookup reads 3 buffers. The gap grows with key length, because hash entries never get wider.

pitfalls.title: Many duplicates in one key
pitfalls.fix: Use hash indexes for unique or nearly unique columns. Exclude the hot values with a partial index (`WHERE status <> 'done'`), or use a B-tree, which deduplicates.

pitfalls.title: Expecting it to shrink or to be smaller
pitfalls.fix: Rebuild with `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. Measure with `pg_relation_size` before choosing hash over B-tree for short keys.

pitfalls.title: Using it for anything but =
pitfalls.fix: Keep hash indexes for equality-only access paths. Everything else needs a B-tree.

keyPointers: Stores a **4-byte hash** per row, sorted by hash within each page. Every match is **lossy** and rechecked against the heap.
bucket = **hash & highmask**, folded with **lowmask** if above `maxbucket`. The masks live in the metapage, cached by each backend.
Growth is **linear hashing**: when `ntuples > ffactor × buckets`, exactly one bucket splits, in the foreground.
Page kinds: **metapage**, **bucket**, **overflow** (chained duplicates), **bitmap** (free overflow pages).
`=` only, single column, no UNIQUE, never shrinks without REINDEX. Best for long, nearly unique keys.

lessons.title: GIN: inverted indexes
lessons.tldr: A GIN index stores each **key** that occurs inside a composite value (array element, jsonb path, text-search lexeme) exactly once, with a sorted **posting list** of the rows that contain it. That inverted layout makes "which rows contain these elements?" fast, and the **pending list** exists because a single row insert would otherwise touch one entry per element.

visualizer.title: Inside a GIN index on tags
visualizer.interaction: Insert rows and watch them queue in the pending list, then overflow it or VACUUM it into the entry tree. Popular keys outgrow their posting list into a posting tree. Run the search to see posting lists intersected and the pending list scanned.

presets.label: Entries and pages
presets.lookFor: 5000 rows but only **29 keys** (t0–t19, c0–c6, rare, common). `common` occurs in 4950 rows, too many for a posting list, so it has a **posting tree**: the `{data,leaf,compressed}` page.

presets.label: Containment search
presets.lookFor: GIN finds both keys and intersects their posting lists. GIN only supports **bitmap scans**, so a Bitmap Heap Scan rechecks the rows. The index part reads **5 buffers**.

presets.label: Pending list fills
presets.lookFor: 300 new rows sit in **2 pending pages**, not in the entry tree. The same search now also reads the pending pages: index buffers go from 5 to **7**.

presets.label: Flush the pending list
presets.lookFor: `gin_clean_pending_list` (or VACUUM, or autovacuum's analyze) moves pending entries into the main structure in one bulk pass and returns the number of pages flushed.

presets.label: jsonb_ops vs jsonb_path_ops
presets.lookFor: `jsonb_path_ops` hashes whole paths, so it is smaller but supports only `@>`, `@?` and `@@`. Neither GIN index helps `->> =`: that is a plain equality on an expression and needs a B-tree expression index.

presets.label: Fix ->> with a B-tree
presets.lookFor: Three ways to ask for one SKU. `->> =` is a Seq Scan (cost 172.50). Rewritten as containment it uses the GIN index (about 17). A **B-tree expression index** on `attrs ->> 'sku'` serves the original query as an Index Scan (8.30), and at 128 kB it is less than half the size of the `jsonb_path_ops` index.

presets.label: Substring search with trigrams
presets.lookFor: pg_trgm splits text into 3-character keys, so a GIN index can answer `LIKE '%…%'`, which no B-tree can. The bitmap scan rechecks rows because trigram matches are only candidates.

production.title: A product catalog with p99 insert spikes
production.problem: Most inserts were fast, but every so often one API call took seconds. Those were the inserts that pushed the **pending list** past `gin_pending_list_limit` (4MB) and had to merge it in the foreground. Searches also slowed down between autovacuum runs, because every search scanned the whole pending list.
production.outcome: Cleanup moves from user requests into autovacuum, so the occasional multi-second insert goes away and searches read a short pending list. In the playground, 300 pending rows add 2 buffer reads to every search (5 → 7) until the list is flushed.

pitfalls.title: Expecting GIN to speed up ->> equality
pitfalls.fix: Either rewrite the filter as containment (`data @> '{"email": "x"}'`) or add a B-tree expression index.

pitfalls.title: Reaching for GIN on range columns
pitfalls.fix: Index ranges with GiST (`USING gist (during)`) or SP-GiST. Both support `&&`, `@>` and `<@`, and GiST also backs exclusion constraints and `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` keys.

pitfalls.title: Occasional very slow inserts
pitfalls.fix: Make autovacuum visit the table more often, lower the per-index limit, or set `fastupdate = off` when steady latency matters more than insert throughput.

pitfalls.title: Building GIN indexes slowly
pitfalls.fix: Raise `maintenance_work_mem` for the build session. For bulk loads, drop the GIN index, load, then recreate it.

keyPointers: GIN = an **entry tree** (B-tree over keys) whose leaf entries hold a **posting list** of TIDs, or point to a **posting tree** when the list is too big.
Each key is stored **once**, so repeated elements compress well. GIN supports only **bitmap scans** and never index-only scans.
**fastupdate** (default on) appends new entries to an unsorted **pending list**. VACUUM, autoanalyze, `gin_clean_pending_list()` or exceeding `gin_pending_list_limit` (4MB) merges it.
Every search also scans the pending list. A big list slows reads, and the insert that overflows it pays for the merge.
Opclasses decide the keys: `array_ops`, `jsonb_ops` (default), `jsonb_path_ops` (smaller, `@>` only), `tsvector_ops`, `gin_trgm_ops`.

lessons.title: GiST and SP-GiST
lessons.tldr: **GiST** is a balanced tree whose entries are predicates such as bounding boxes, and **SP-GiST** is an unbalanced tree that splits space into non-overlapping parts such as quadrants, k-d halves or string prefixes. Both are frameworks where an operator class supplies the geometry, so one access method can serve overlap, containment, range, nearest-neighbour `<->` and exclusion-constraint queries that a B-tree cannot express.

visualizer.title: Nearest-neighbour search, box by box
visualizer.interaction: Step a 3-nearest-neighbour search through a GiST R-tree, then through an SP-GiST quad-tree over the same points. Click anywhere to move the query point and compare how many nodes each visits.

presets.label: KNN with GiST
presets.lookFor: `Order By: (loc <-> …)` inside the Index Scan: the index returns rows nearest-first, so 5 neighbours out of 50000 cost about **8 buffers**, with no sort.

presets.label: Box containment
presets.lookFor: The `consistent` function prunes every subtree whose bounding box cannot intersect the query box. The bitmap scan reads only a handful of index pages.

presets.label: SP-GiST quad-tree
presets.lookFor: `quad_point_ops` is the default SP-GiST opclass for `point`. Same KNN plan shape; here it reads about 14 buffers, and the index is smaller (about 2.3 MB vs 3.3 MB for GiST).

presets.label: Exclusion constraint
presets.lookFor: No two rows may have equal `room` **and** overlapping `during`. `btree_gist` supplies GiST support for `=` on int. Back-to-back bookings are fine because `[)` ranges do not overlap. Try inserting 101 at 10:30 to see the conflict error.

presets.label: Temporal primary key (18)
presets.lookFor: PostgreSQL 18 `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` turns the primary key into "no two rows for the same product whose periods overlap". The backing index is a **GiST** index (`USING gist (product_id, valid)`), the same machinery as an exclusion constraint. Try `INSERT INTO prices VALUES (1, tstzrange('2025-06-01', '2025-09-01'), 31);`: it fails with SQLSTATE **23P01**, an exclusion violation, not 23505.

presets.label: Operator classes
presets.lookFor: For `point`: GiST `point_ops`, SP-GiST `quad_point_ops` (default) and `kd_point_ops`. Choosing an opclass chooses the tree shape.

production.title: Double-booked meeting rooms
production.problem: Two users clicking "book" at the same moment both passed the check, because neither saw the other's uncommitted row. The result was a few double bookings every week and support tickets to fix them by hand.
production.outcome: Overlapping inserts now fail with SQLSTATE `23P01` (exclusion_violation), which the app turns into a "slot just taken" message. The same index also speeds up "what is booked in this room this week" queries.

pitfalls.title: Ordering by distance without the index operator
pitfalls.fix: Write `ORDER BY loc <-> $1 LIMIT k` so EXPLAIN shows `Order By:` inside the index scan.

pitfalls.title: Missing btree_gist for mixed exclusion constraints
pitfalls.fix: `CREATE EXTENSION btree_gist;` then create the constraint.

pitfalls.title: Catching 23505 for a temporal or exclusion key
pitfalls.fix: Handle both codes. In PL/pgSQL, catch `exclusion_violation` alongside `unique_violation`. Temporal keys also reject empty ranges, so validate input ranges before inserting.

pitfalls.title: Assuming GiST behaves like a B-tree
pitfalls.fix: For point data that is partitioned naturally, try SP-GiST (no overlap). Compare buffers with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and rebuild with REINDEX after heavy churn.

keyPointers: **GiST**: balanced, entries are predicates (e.g. bounding boxes). Support functions: `consistent`, `union`, `penalty`, `picksplit`, `same`, plus optional `distance` for KNN.
**SP-GiST**: unbalanced space partitioning (quad-tree, k-d tree, radix tree). Regions never overlap. `quad_point_ops` is the default for point.
KNN: `ORDER BY col <-> value LIMIT k` walks the tree best-first with lower-bound distances, so it never sorts the table.
Exclusion constraints (`EXCLUDE USING gist (… WITH &&)`) generalise UNIQUE to "no two rows overlap". `btree_gist` adds `=` for scalars.
Both are lossy per opclass: `Recheck Cond` and `Rows Removed by Index Recheck` show rows re-tested against the heap.

lessons.title: BRIN for huge append-only tables
lessons.tldr: A BRIN index stores one tiny **summary** (such as the min and max value) per **block range** of consecutive heap pages, so it stays a few kilobytes even for a table of gigabytes. When a column follows the physical row order, as timestamps do in an append-only log, those summaries let a scan skip almost every block for the cost of reading a handful of index pages.

visualizer.title: Block ranges, summaries and what a query must read
visualizer.interaction: Slide the query window and watch which ranges are consistent with it. Then add outliers, shuffle the rows, change `pages_per_range`, append unsummarized blocks, and compare minmax with minmax-multi.

presets.label: Tiny index
presets.lookFor: 1082 heap pages need only **68** range summaries (16 pages each): 24 kB of BRIN against about 4.4 MB of B-tree. `correlation` is 1 for `readings` and close to 0 for `shuffled`.

presets.label: Read the summaries
presets.lookFor: Each tuple covers 16 blocks starting at `blknum`. In `readings` each summary spans about 8 hours. In `shuffled` every summary spans the whole 23 days, so it can never exclude anything.

presets.label: Lossy bitmap scan
presets.lookFor: `Heap Blocks: lossy=16`: one matching range, all 16 of its pages read. `Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 2600` are the rows on those pages outside the hour. About 21 buffers in total.

presets.label: Uncorrelated: useless
presets.lookFor: Same query, same index type, shuffled rows: every range matches, so the planner does a **Seq Scan** of all 1088 pages.

presets.label: New rows: unsummarized
presets.lookFor: Pages appended after the index was built have no summary until VACUUM, `autosummarize`, or `brin_summarize_new_values()` processes them. Until then every scan must read them. Here 68 summaries become **75**.

presets.label: minmax-multi and bloom
presets.lookFor: **minmax-multi** stores several intervals per range (good with outliers). **bloom** stores a Bloom filter for equality on values that are not ordered. Both are still lossy.

production.title: Indexing a 2-billion-row sensor table without doubling its size
production.problem: A B-tree on `ts` was larger than a fifth of the table, every insert had to update it, and it no longer fit in memory. Dropping it made window queries scan the whole table.
production.outcome: In the playground the BRIN index is 24 kB against 4.4 MB for a B-tree on the same 200000 rows (about 180× smaller), and a one-hour query reads 21 buffers instead of 1088. Inserts barely touch the index, because a range's summary changes only when a new value widens it.

pitfalls.title: BRIN on a column that does not follow physical order
pitfalls.fix: Check `correlation` in `pg_stats` (close to ±1 is good). Use BRIN only for append-mostly data, or physically order the table first (`CLUSTER` with a B-tree, then switch).

pitfalls.title: Freshly inserted ranges are never skipped
pitfalls.fix: Create the index `WITH (autosummarize = on)` or call `brin_summarize_new_values()` from your loader.

pitfalls.title: Outliers and backfills widen ranges
pitfalls.fix: Use `minmax-multi` opclasses, or `brin_desummarize_range()` plus re-summarize after fixing the data.

keyPointers: One index tuple per **block range** (`pages_per_range`, default **128** pages). Index size ≈ table pages / pages_per_range.
BRIN scans are always **bitmap** and always **lossy**: every page of a matching range is read and every row rechecked.
Useful only when values follow **physical order** (`pg_stats.correlation` near ±1): append-only logs, time series, IoT.
Opclass kinds: **minmax**, **minmax-multi** (outliers), **inclusion** (ranges, boxes, inet), **bloom** (equality).
New ranges stay unsummarized until VACUUM, `autosummarize = on` (default off) or `brin_summarize_new_values()`.

lessons.title: Designing indexes: multicolumn, partial, expression, covering
lessons.tldr: A good index matches how one important query filters and sorts: **equality columns first and the range column last**, a **predicate** for the rows you actually query, the **same expression** the WHERE clause uses, and **INCLUDE** columns so the heap is never read. Each extra index slows every write and can block HOT updates, so the goal is the smallest set of indexes that turns your hot queries into short, ordered index reads.

visualizer.title: Pick the index: five real queries
visualizer.interaction: For each query, choose one of three candidate indexes. The answer shows the real plan, buffers and index size PostgreSQL 18 produced for that index alone.

presets.label: Equality first, range last
presets.lookFor: Both conditions appear in `Index Cond`, and the scan reads only user 42's February entries: about 5 buffers.

presets.label: Skip scan (18)
presets.lookFor: Run 1 uses `(region, category, sale_date)` without any condition on `region`. That is a **skip scan**, new in PostgreSQL 18, and it shows `Index Searches: 7`. Run 2 names the three regions and needs only 3 searches. Run 3, with an index that leads with the filtered columns, needs 1. Skip scan rescues an index whose leading column has few distinct values. It does not replace the right column order.

presets.label: Partial index
presets.lookFor: 32 kB, ordered, and only pending rows. The planner uses it only when the query's WHERE **implies** the predicate: the `status = 'done'` query cannot use it.

presets.label: Expression index
presets.lookFor: Before: Seq Scan with a `lower()` Filter. After creating the index and running ANALYZE (which collects statistics for the expression), the row estimate is right and the index is used.

presets.label: A cast hides the index
presets.lookFor: `int = bigint` still uses the index, because both types belong to the same B-tree operator family. `42.0` is `numeric`, so PostgreSQL casts the **column**: `Filter: ((user_id)::numeric = 42.0)` and a Seq Scan costing 2531 instead of 76. Casting the column to text does the same thing. Match the literal to the column type.

presets.label: INCLUDE and heap fetches
presets.lookFor: First run: `Heap Fetches: 0`, 15 buffers. The UPDATE clears the all-visible bits of the pages it touched, so the second run visits the heap: **4120 heap fetches**, more than the 4020 rows, because the non-HOT update left old index entries pointing at dead versions. VACUUM fixes both.

presets.label: NULLS NOT DISTINCT
presets.lookFor: By default NULLs are distinct, so two `(1, NULL)` rows are allowed. With `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` a second `(1, NULL)` would violate the index. Try inserting it again.

presets.label: Unused indexes
presets.lookFor: Statistics are flushed lazily; the first call forces it. `idx_scan = 0` over a long period means the index costs write time and space without serving reads. Check replicas too before dropping it. The second query is the usual "index usage %" check. It needs `NULLIF` against division by zero, and `coalesce` because `idx_scan` is NULL for a table with no indexes. Only trust it on large tables: seq scans on tiny tables are correct.

production.title: A job queue that slowed down as it grew
production.problem: The only index was on `state`. Each poll found all queued rows, fetched them from the heap and sorted them to keep ten. A full index on `run_at` alone would have walked millions of finished jobs before finding queued ones.
production.outcome: In the playground's smaller version (500 pending of 100000 rows) the same change cuts the poll from 503 buffers with a sort to 12 buffers without one, using a 32 kB index instead of 700 kB.

pitfalls.title: Range column first in a composite index
pitfalls.fix: Order key columns as: equality columns, then at most one range or ORDER BY column. Verify with buffers in `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`.

pitfalls.title: Partial index never chosen with parameters
pitfalls.fix: Write the predicate as a literal in the query (`WHERE status = 'pending'`), or use custom plans (`plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan`).

pitfalls.title: CREATE INDEX on a busy table
pitfalls.fix: Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` outside a transaction block. On failure, `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` the invalid index or `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY` it.

pitfalls.title: Indexes that block HOT updates
pitfalls.fix: Avoid indexing columns that change constantly (counters, `updated_at`) unless a key query needs them. Watch `n_tup_hot_upd` in `pg_stat_user_tables`.

pitfalls.title: Assuming foreign keys are indexed
pitfalls.fix: Index the referencing columns of every foreign key that sees parent deletes or joins. This catalog query lists foreign keys whose first column leads no index.

pitfalls.title: Expression index on a cast that is not immutable
pitfalls.fix: Store the value in a real `timestamptz` column written by the application or a trigger (a generated column has the same immutability rule), or store an immutable form such as epoch seconds and index `((doc->>'ts')::float8)`. Then write the query with exactly the same expression.

keyPointers: B-tree rule: **equality on leading columns + one range** on the next column bound the scan. PostgreSQL 18 **skip scan** helps when a leading column has few distinct values.
**Partial** indexes need the query to imply the predicate at plan time. Great for queues, soft deletes and rare states.
**Expression** indexes match only the identical expression. Run ANALYZE after creating one.
**INCLUDE** columns enable index-only scans (needs all-visible pages, i.e. VACUUM). INCLUDE indexes are never deduplicated.
Unique indexes treat NULLs as distinct unless `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`. Build with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and check for INVALID leftovers.

lessons.title: Reading EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
lessons.tldr: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query and prints the plan tree with each node's **estimated** cost and rows next to its **actual** time, rows, loops and (by default in PostgreSQL 18) **buffers**. Reading it bottom-up shows where time and I/O really go, and the gaps between estimates and reality point straight at the statistics, indexes or memory settings to fix.

visualizer.title: Click through seven real plans
visualizer.interaction: Pick a scenario and click any node, or press Next node to tour the tree. Compare the in-memory and spilled sort, 1 and 2 hash batches, and an index-only scan before and after VACUUM.

presets.label: Node anatomy
presets.lookFor: Read bottom-up: two scans feed a Hash Join, which feeds HashAggregate. Each line shows `(cost=… rows=…)` then `(actual time=… rows=… loops=…)`. Buffers appear without asking: BUFFERS is on by default with ANALYZE in 18.

presets.label: Filter becomes Index Cond
presets.lookFor: Before: `Seq Scan`, `Filter`, `Rows Removed by Filter: 4999`, cost 94.50 and 32 buffers. After: `Index Scan`, `Index Cond`, cost 8.30 and 3 buffers. A **Filter** is checked on every row after it is read. An **Index Cond** decides which rows are read at all. The IN list shows `Index Searches: 3`.

presets.label: Sort spill
presets.lookFor: `Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 2128kB` with `temp read/written` buffers, versus `quicksort  Memory: 5174kB`. The fix is memory for that query, not an index.

presets.label: Hash batches
presets.lookFor: `Batches: 2` on the Hash node: the inner side did not fit in `work_mem × hash_mem_multiplier` (2.0), so it went to temp files and was processed in two passes.

presets.label: Loops multiply
presets.lookFor: The inner Bitmap Heap Scan shows `rows=20.00 loops=3`: 60 rows in total. `Index Searches: 3` counts one descent per loop.

presets.label: Heap fetches → 0
presets.lookFor: Before VACUUM: `Heap Fetches: 6020` and about 6028 buffers. After VACUUM sets the visibility map: `Heap Fetches: 0` and 9 buffers. Same plan shape, a 600× difference in I/O.

presets.label: Misestimate
presets.lookFor: An expression the planner has no statistics for gets a default selectivity, here **10 rows estimated, 199 actual**. Compare the two `rows=` values on each line first: everything above a misestimate is planned on wrong numbers.

presets.label: JSON and settings
presets.lookFor: `SETTINGS` lists planner-relevant settings that differ from defaults: `work_mem`, and also `max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0`, which is why the playground never shows parallel plans. `FORMAT JSON` is what plan visualizers parse. The `Sort Method` is `top-N heapsort`: LIMIT keeps only 10 rows, so no spill.

production.title: A nightly report that took 40 minutes
production.problem: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` showed a Hash node with **Batches: 64** and gigabytes of temp writes, then a Sort with **external merge**. The server ran with the default `work_mem` of 4MB, so every hash and sort spilled to disk.
production.outcome: In the playground the same effect is visible at small scale: the sort goes from external merge with 1636 temp blocks to an in-memory quicksort, and the hash join from 2 batches to 1. Spill-free plans also stop competing for disk with daytime traffic.

pitfalls.title: Reading per-loop numbers as totals
pitfalls.fix: Multiply time and rows by `loops`. Look for the node whose time × loops dominates. Buffers, unlike rows, are already totals.

pitfalls.title: Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on writes
pitfalls.fix: Wrap it in a transaction and roll back.

pitfalls.title: Blaming the wrong node
pitfalls.fix: Subtract children's times to find each node's own work, or use a visualizer that does it. Start from the deepest node whose estimate first diverges from actual rows.

pitfalls.title: Index-only scans that are not
pitfalls.fix: VACUUM the table (or tune autovacuum for insert-heavy tables with `autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor`) so pages become all-visible.

pitfalls.title: Looking for EXPLAIN options that do not exist
pitfalls.fix: For I/O, read the `Buffers:` lines (automatic with ANALYZE in 18), and set `track_io_timing = on` to add `I/O Timings`. Use `BUFFERS OFF` to hide them. For CPU time, compare `actual time` with the I/O timings.

keyPointers: Each node: `(cost=startup..total rows= width=)` estimated, then `(actual time=first..last rows= loops=)` measured. **Compare the two rows values first.**
Actual rows and time are **per loop**; multiply by `loops`. A node's time includes its children.
**Buffers** (default with ANALYZE in 18): shared hit = cached, read = from OS, temp = spills. They include child nodes.
Red flags: `external merge Disk`, `Batches` > 1, `Heap Fetches` > 0, big `Rows Removed by Filter`, `lossy` heap blocks.
Not shown in the playground but common in production: `Gather` with `Workers Planned/Launched` for parallel query, and a `JIT:` block when the plan cost exceeds `jit_above_cost`.

modules.title: Concurrency, MVCC & Locking
modules.summary: Snapshots and visibility rules, HOT updates, isolation levels, and the lock hierarchy from spinlocks to table locks.

lessons.title: ACID and transactions
lessons.tldr: A **transaction** groups statements so they commit or vanish together, and PostgreSQL implements that by stamping every row version with an **xid** and recording one 2-bit status per xid in the commit log. Because rollback and crash recovery only have to flip or ignore that status, an abort is instant and PostgreSQL needs **no undo log**.

visualizer.title: A transfer with a savepoint, xid by xid
visualizer.interaction: Step through BEGIN, two UPDATEs, a SAVEPOINT and a ROLLBACK TO. Switch the ending to compare a clean COMMIT, a crash, and an error followed by COMMIT.

presets.label: Virtual vs real xid
presets.lookFor: Before the UPDATE the xid is **NULL**: only a virtual xid exists. After it, a `transactionid` lock on the new xid appears, held in the main lock table (`fastpath = false`).

presets.label: Savepoint = subtransaction
presets.lookFor: Two `transactionid` locks: the top xid and a **subxid** one higher. Bob's new version has `cmin = 1`. After `ROLLBACK TO`, bob's surviving row shows `xmax` = the aborted subxid, which readers ignore.

presets.label: Transfer: all or nothing
presets.lookFor: The first CALL commits inside the procedure: alice **70**, bob **80**. The negative transfer fails on the credit (**23514**) and alice's debit vanishes with it. Inside a transaction block the procedure may not COMMIT, so CALL fails with **2D000** `invalid transaction termination`.

presets.label: Transactional DDL
presets.lookFor: The third ALTER fails (**23502**: existing rows have no postal code), and the first two columns are rolled back with it: `new_columns = 0`. Schema changes are ordinary transactional writes to the catalogs.

presets.label: Read the commit log
presets.lookFor: Every version ever written is still on the page. `pg_xact_status` reads `pg_xact`: versions whose xmin is **aborted** are invisible forever, and an aborted xmax deletes nothing.

presets.label: Sequences ignore ROLLBACK
presets.lookFor: The rollback did not give back 1 and 2, and the failed INSERT used up **3** before its CHECK fired, so the first real invoice is number **4**. Sequences are non-transactional by design, which is what lets concurrent sessions take values without waiting.

presets.label: Cost of subtransactions
presets.lookFor: Each `BEGIN … EXCEPTION` block is a subtransaction, and each one that writes burns a **subxid**: the 500-row loop advances the counter by about 500. The set-based UPDATE uses one xid.

presets.label: Implicit transactions & 2PC
presets.lookFor: A plain read gets no xid (**NULL**). `txid_current()` forces one, and outside BEGIN each statement is its own transaction, so the two values differ by one. `max_prepared_transactions = 0` disables `PREPARE TRANSACTION`; production 2PC needs it raised.

production.title: A nightly job that burned half a million xids
production.problem: Every exception block is a **subtransaction**, and every one that writes gets its own subxid. One run over 500 k accounts assigns about 500 k subxids inside one top-level transaction. Past **64 cached subxids** per backend, other sessions' visibility checks must consult `pg_subtrans`, and the xid counter races toward the freeze thresholds.
production.outcome: On 500 rows the per-row exception loop advances the xid counter by **502**, the set-based UPDATE by **1**. The subxid cache can no longer overflow, and xid consumption drops by the row count.

pitfalls.title: Idle in transaction
pitfalls.fix: Commit or roll back after every unit of work (reads included), and set a server-side guard.

pitfalls.title: Subtransaction overflow
pitfalls.fix: Avoid per-row savepoints (ORM "nested transactions", PL/pgSQL EXCEPTION inside loops). Batch the work set-based, or commit in smaller transactions.

pitfalls.title: Carrying on after an error
pitfalls.fix: Check every statement result and ROLLBACK on error, then retry the unit of work. To survive an expected failure inside one transaction, set a SAVEPOINT before it and `ROLLBACK TO` it on error.

pitfalls.title: A procedure that COMMITs, called inside BEGIN
pitfalls.fix: Run such procedures in autocommit mode, as a top-level CALL. If the caller must own the transaction, remove COMMIT from the procedure and let the caller commit.

pitfalls.title: Expecting ROLLBACK to undo everything
pitfalls.fix: Never use a sequence as a gap-free counter. Use `pg_advisory_xact_lock` when the lock should end with the transaction.

pitfalls.title: Forgotten prepared transactions
pitfalls.fix: Leave `max_prepared_transactions = 0` unless you run a transaction manager, and alert on old rows in `pg_prepared_xacts`.

keyPointers: Every transaction has a **virtual xid**. A real **xid** (32-bit, wraps; `xid8` adds the epoch) is assigned only at the first write.
Commit and abort are a **2-bit status** per xid in `pg_xact`. Rows are never undone: aborted xmins are invisible and aborted xmaxes are ignored.
**SAVEPOINT** and PL/pgSQL **EXCEPTION** blocks are subtransactions with their own **subxids**. Only 64 are cached per backend.
Locks are held to **transaction end**, except those taken after a savepoint that is rolled back to.
**2PC**: `PREPARE TRANSACTION` → `COMMIT PREPARED` / `ROLLBACK PREPARED`; inspect `pg_prepared_xacts`.

lessons.title: Snapshots and tuple visibility
lessons.tldr: A **snapshot** is three numbers, `xmin:xmax:xip`, that classify every xid as finished, in progress, or not yet started, and a row version is visible when its inserting xid counts and its deleting xid does not. Snapshots let readers and writers work on the same rows at once without blocking, because each reader just ignores the versions its snapshot cannot see.

visualizer.title: Two sessions, one row, two isolation levels
visualizer.interaction: Step the timeline, then flip A to Repeatable Read and replay it. Below, edit a snapshot and click xids to see the visibility rule decide.

presets.label: Your snapshot
presets.lookFor: With only one session, nothing is in progress: `xmin = xmax` and `xip` is empty. `my_xid` is NULL because this read-only statement never needed an xid.

presets.label: UPDATE writes a new version
