presets.lookFor: DELETE left **5,000 dead rows** in 64 pages for VACUUM. TRUNCATE swapped in a new empty file (new filenode, 0 bytes) and left nothing to clean, but it holds **AccessExclusiveLock** until COMMIT. Roll it back and the old file comes back.

production.title: An audit table that was "fixed" nightly with VACUUM FULL
production.problem: VACUUM FULL took over 40 minutes and held ACCESS EXCLUSIVE the whole time, so every API call that wrote an audit row queued behind it and timed out. It also needed about 120 GB of free disk for the copy.
production.outcome: The table settles at its steady-state size (about 90 days of data plus one day of churn) without ever going offline. Plain VACUUM runs alongside writes, needs no extra disk, and with partitions the nightly purge becomes a metadata change.

pitfalls.title: Running VACUUM FULL in business hours
pitfalls.fix: Use plain VACUUM for routine work. If only the indexes are bloated, `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY` rebuilds one online under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE (if it fails, it leaves an INVALID index to drop). To shrink the table itself online, use an extension such as pg_repack, or rebuild into a new table and swap.

pitfalls.title: A long transaction makes VACUUM useless
pitfalls.fix: Find and end the oldest snapshot holders; set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`.

pitfalls.title: Expecting plain VACUUM to shrink the file
pitfalls.fix: That is usually what you want. If the table will stay small, rewrite it once in a maintenance window, or partition so you can drop whole chunks.

pitfalls.title: VACUUM from application code fails
pitfalls.fix: Switch that connection to autocommit before sending VACUUM, and never wrap it in BEGIN, a function or a DO block.

pitfalls.title: Treating TRUNCATE as a cheap DELETE
pitfalls.fix: Use TRUNCATE for tables nobody else is reading at that moment. Keep its transaction short, and set `lock_timeout` so it gives up instead of queueing everyone behind it.

keyPointers: Plain VACUUM: **SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE**, runs online, space is **reused**, only the empty tail goes back to the OS.
Phases: **scan heap (prune, collect dead TIDs) → vacuum indexes → vacuum heap → clean up indexes → truncate → final cleanup**.
Dead TIDs must fit in **`maintenance_work_mem`**, or indexes are scanned more than once.
VACUUM sets **all-visible / all-frozen** bits and fills the **FSM**; DELETE does neither.
VACUUM FULL: **ACCESS EXCLUSIVE**, new relfilenode, rebuilt indexes, needs disk for a full copy.

lessons.title: Tuning autovacuum
lessons.tldr: **Autovacuum** is a launcher plus a few worker processes that vacuum and analyze each table once its counts of dead, inserted or changed rows cross a threshold computed from the table size. The defaults suit small tables, so big or hot tables need per-table thresholds and a larger I/O budget, or dead rows pile up faster than the throttled workers can remove them.

visualizer.title: When autovacuum fires, and how fast it can work
visualizer.interaction: Pick a scenario or drag the sliders: the trigger formulas update, and a 24-hour simulation shows dead rows and runs. Switch to **How fast can it go?** for the cost-based throttle.

presets.label: The global knobs
presets.lookFor: New in 18: `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold` (100 M), and `autovacuum_worker_slots` (16) next to `autovacuum_max_workers` (3). Slots reserve shared memory and need a restart; `max_workers` is reloadable up to the slot count. `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = -1` means "use `vacuum_cost_limit`" (200).

presets.label: When will this table be vacuumed?
presets.lookFor: With 20,000 rows the dead-row trigger is 50 + 0.2 × 20,000 = **4,050**. The `av_status` view in the setup applies the trigger formulas, including per-table overrides.

presets.label: Churn rows past the trigger
presets.lookFor: 3,000 dead rows: not yet. 5,000: due. On a server the launcher would start a worker within `autovacuum_naptime` (1 min). This playground runs no autovacuum, so nothing happens by itself here.

presets.label: Per-table override
presets.lookFor: Now 1000 + 0.01 × 20,000 = **1,200**. Storage parameters beat the global settings for this table only.

presets.label: Insert-only tables and freezing
presets.lookFor: The insert trigger scales with the **unfrozen** share of the table. After VACUUM FREEZE every page is all-frozen, so the trigger falls to the base **1,000** instead of 1000 + 0.2 × 30,000 = 7,000. (`relpages` and `relallfrozen` refresh only at the next VACUUM or ANALYZE.)

presets.label: Throttle arithmetic
presets.lookFor: At defaults one worker can read about 390 MB/s from disk but only about 35 MB/s when it also dirties every page. That budget is shared by all running workers.

presets.label: Health check and 18's timing columns
presets.lookFor: The dead-row share uses `NULLIF` so an empty table does not divide by zero. The `total_*_time` columns (milliseconds, new in 18) show where vacuum time goes; `autovacuum_ms` stays 0 here because nothing runs automatically. A per-table `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold = 500` caps the trigger at **500** dead rows.

production.title: A 200 M-row orders table that bloated between vacuums
production.problem: With the default scale factor, autovacuum waited for 50 + 0.2 × 200 M = **40 M** dead rows. That took about 17 hours of updates to reach, so heap and indexes carried up to 20% dead rows between runs, and every run had 40 M index entries to remove. Queries slowed as scans read through dead rows.
production.outcome: The trigger drops from 40 M to about 2 M dead rows: roughly one run every 50 minutes at peak instead of one every 17 hours, and each run has 20× less to clean. Dead rows stay near 1% of the table.

pitfalls.title: Big tables wait for 20% of their rows to die
pitfalls.fix: Lower `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` per table (0.01 to 0.05 for big, hot tables), or lower `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold`.

pitfalls.title: Autovacuum keeps getting cancelled
pitfalls.fix: Stop the frequent conflicting command, or run a manual `VACUUM` in a quiet window. Check `pg_stat_user_tables.autovacuum_count` to confirm runs complete.

pitfalls.title: Adding workers does not make vacuum faster
pitfalls.fix: Raise `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` (or lower the delay) together with the worker count, within what the disks can sustain.

pitfalls.title: Partitioned parents are never auto-analyzed
pitfalls.fix: Run `ANALYZE parent_table` after large loads and on a schedule.

pitfalls.title: Hunting autovacuum workers by query text
pitfalls.fix: Filter on `backend_type`, grant the predefined role to the migration user, and remember that an anti-wraparound run will simply restart.

keyPointers: Vacuum when dead rows > **min(max_threshold, 50 + 0.2 × reltuples)**; max_threshold (100 M) is **new in 18**.
Insert-only tables: **1000 + 0.2 × reltuples × unfrozen share**; analyze: **50 + 0.1 × reltuples**.
Override per table with **storage parameters** (`ALTER TABLE … SET (autovacuum_…)`).
Throttle: **cost_limit 200** per **2 ms** delay, page hit 1 / miss 2 / dirty 20, **shared by all workers**.
Watch **`pg_stat_user_tables`**: `n_dead_tup`, `n_ins_since_vacuum`, `last_autovacuum`, `autovacuum_count`.

lessons.title: XID wraparound, freezing and MultiXacts
lessons.tldr: Transaction IDs are 32-bit counters compared modulo 2^32, so any row whose `xmin` falls more than about 2 billion transactions behind would suddenly look like it came from the future. VACUUM prevents that by **freezing** old rows, marking them older than every XID, and PostgreSQL escalates from aggressive vacuums to forced autovacuums to refusing new XIDs as a table approaches the limit.

visualizer.title: The XID circle
visualizer.interaction: Advance through each threshold and watch what the server does. Run VACUUM to freeze and pull `relfrozenxid` forward, then switch to **What if nothing froze?** and push past 2^31.

presets.label: How old is everything?
presets.lookFor: The three ages to monitor: per table, including its TOAST table, and per database. `pg_current_xact_id()` returns a 64-bit `xid8` (epoch + xid); the on-disk xmin is the low 32 bits.

presets.label: Which statements use an XID?
presets.lookFor: A transaction gets an XID only when it first **writes**: reads alone leave it NULL, so read traffic never ages the cluster. `txid_current()` and `pg_current_xact_id()` force one, so each probe call burns an XID (they differ by 1).

presets.label: Burn 100,000 XIDs
presets.lookFor: Each loop commits once, so each consumes one XID. `relfrozenxid` stays put and its age grows. Busy servers burn this many in seconds to minutes.

presets.label: Not frozen yet
presets.lookFor: Rows still carry their original xmin and no `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN` flag. No page is all-frozen.

presets.label: VACUUM (FREEZE)
presets.lookFor: `relfrozenxid` jumps forward and its age drops to almost 0. Each tuple shows `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN`, yet `t_xmin` keeps its original value: freezing sets flag bits, it no longer overwrites xmin.

presets.label: The freeze settings
presets.lookFor: 50 M, 150 M, 200 M and 1.6 B for XIDs; multixacts have their own, larger limits (5 M, 150 M, 400 M).

presets.label: Make a MultiXact
presets.lookFor: Two lockers on one row do not fit in `xmax`, so `xmax` holds a **MultiXact ID** (`HEAP_XMAX_IS_MULTI`) and its members live in `pg_multixact`. MultiXact IDs wrap around too.

production.title: A forgotten replication slot and the wraparound countdown
production.problem: Monitoring showed `age(datfrozenxid)` climbing past 1 billion although autovacuum ran constantly. The slot's `catalog_xmin` pinned the oldest XID that VACUUM could freeze past. At 3,000 XIDs/s, about 1.1 billion remaining XIDs is roughly 4 days until the 40 M warning zone.
production.outcome: Once the slot was dropped, the next aggressive vacuums advanced `relfrozenxid`, and `age(datfrozenxid)` fell back to around the 200 M `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` range. An alert on `age(datfrozenxid) > 500 M` and on inactive slots now catches this weeks earlier.

pitfalls.title: Panicking into single-user mode
pitfalls.fix: Stay online. Clear prepared transactions, long transactions and stale slots, then run a plain database-wide `VACUUM` as superuser. Do not use VACUUM FULL (it needs an XID) or VACUUM FREEZE (more work than needed).

pitfalls.title: An idle-in-transaction session blocks freezing
pitfalls.fix: Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` and alert on old `backend_xmin`.

pitfalls.title: Insert-only tables surprise you with a huge vacuum
pitfalls.fix: Let insert-triggered autovacuum freeze as you go (keep `autovacuum_vacuum_insert_threshold` enabled, consider a lower per-table `autovacuum_freeze_min_age`), or run `VACUUM (FREEZE)` after bulk loads.

pitfalls.title: A health check that burns XIDs
pitfalls.fix: Probe with `SELECT 1`, or read the current value without assigning one: `pg_current_snapshot()` or `pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned()`.

keyPointers: XIDs are **32-bit, compared modulo 2^32**: 2 billion in the past, 2 billion in the future.
**Freezing** marks a row older than every XID; `relfrozenxid` / `datfrozenxid` track the oldest unfrozen XID.
Ladder: **150 M** aggressive · **200 M** forced autovacuum · **1.6 B** failsafe · **40 M before wrap** warnings · **3 M before wrap** no new XIDs.
Recovery: end prepared/long transactions, drop stale slots, plain **VACUUM** as superuser; never single-user mode, FULL or FREEZE.
**MultiXacts** (several lockers in one `xmax`) age and wrap the same way: watch `mxid_age(relminmxid)`.

lessons.title: Physical streaming replication
lessons.tldr: A **standby** is a copy of the primary that stays in permanent recovery, receiving the primary's WAL over a replication connection and replaying it byte for byte. Streaming gives a second server for failover and read queries, and **synchronous replication** lets a COMMIT wait until a standby has written, flushed or replayed its WAL.

visualizer.title: A primary streaming to a hot standby
visualizer.interaction: Press **COMMIT** and watch WAL travel out and replies come back. Change the `synchronous_commit` level, the latency, cut the network, or start a long standby query. The standby is simulated: the playground database is a single process.

presets.label: Replication settings
presets.lookFor: `wal_level = replica` is enough for physical standbys. `max_slot_wal_keep_size = -1` means a slot may retain unlimited WAL. The standby-side settings are listed too; they only matter on a standby.

presets.label: Create a physical slot
presets.lookFor: The second argument reserves WAL immediately. A standby would use it with `primary_slot_name = 'standby_a'`.

presets.label: Write WAL nobody consumes
presets.lookFor: With no standby attached, `restart_lsn` never moves, so every byte written since is pinned in `pg_wal`. `safe_wal_size` is NULL because `max_slot_wal_keep_size` is unlimited.

presets.label: What a lag query computes
presets.lookFor: Each gap points at a different bottleneck: network, standby disk, or replay (often a query conflict). `write_lag`, `flush_lag` and `replay_lag` give the same stages as time.

presets.label: Recovery functions on a primary
presets.lookFor: On a primary the standby-side functions return NULL. On a standby, `now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()` is a common lag-in-time check.

presets.label: Drop the slot
presets.lookFor: Dropping an unused slot releases the retained WAL at the next checkpoint. Forgotten slots are the classic cause of a full `pg_wal`.

production.title: Synchronous replication without single-standby hangs
production.problem: They started with `synchronous_standby_names = 's1'`. During a routine restart of s1, every write transaction on the primary hung at COMMIT for the whole maintenance window, because the only synchronous standby was gone.
production.outcome: Either standby can now confirm a commit, so restarting one no longer blocks writes, and an acknowledged payment is still on durable storage in a second zone. Commit latency is one round trip to the nearest healthy standby plus its fsync.

pitfalls.title: An inactive slot fills pg_wal
pitfalls.fix: Alert on inactive slots and retained bytes, drop slots you no longer need, and set `max_slot_wal_keep_size` so a dead standby is invalidated instead of taking the primary down.

pitfalls.title: Standby queries cancelled with "conflict with recovery"
pitfalls.fix: Enable `hot_standby_feedback` (costs some bloat on the primary), raise `max_standby_streaming_delay` on reporting standbys, or move long reports to a dedicated delayed replica.

pitfalls.title: Both nodes think they are primary
pitfalls.fix: Fence the old primary (STONITH) before promoting, and use a cluster manager. Rejoin the old primary as a standby with `pg_rewind` instead of a full re-clone.

keyPointers: **walsender** (primary) streams WAL to the **walreceiver** (standby); the **startup process** replays it.
Positions: **sent → write → flush → replay**; `pg_stat_replication` shows each LSN and the matching **lag**.
Slots keep WAL (and with feedback, old rows) until the standby has it; cap with **`max_slot_wal_keep_size`**.
`synchronous_standby_names` = `FIRST n (…)` or `ANY n (…)`; `synchronous_commit` picks **remote_write / on / remote_apply**.
Hot standby is read-only; conflicts are resolved by **delaying replay** up to `max_standby_streaming_delay`, then cancelling.

lessons.title: Logical replication
lessons.tldr: **Logical replication** decodes the WAL back into row-level INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE messages and streams them, per table, from a **publication** to a **subscription** on another server. Unlike physical streaming it can replicate a subset of tables, rows and columns, across major versions and platforms, into a database that stays writable.

visualizer.title: From WAL records to filtered row changes
visualizer.interaction: Step through four interleaved transactions: decoding, the reorder buffer, commit order, an abort, and a publication with a row filter and column list. Then flip old and new values below.

presets.label: Publication with a row filter and column list
presets.lookFor: An INSERT-only publication may filter on any column. `total` and `card_last4` are not in the column list, so they never leave the publisher (but a column list is not a security boundary).

presets.label: Replica identity
presets.lookFor: UPDATE and DELETE messages identify the old row by its replica identity. `clicks` has no primary key, so its default identity is empty.

presets.label: Publishing UPDATEs needs an identity
presets.lookFor: The error is raised **on the publisher**, even with no subscriber attached. `FULL` fixes it, at the cost of logging whole old rows and slow row lookups on the subscriber.

presets.label: Row filters must use identity columns
presets.lookFor: A publication that sends UPDATEs must evaluate the filter on the old row, so it may only reference replica identity columns. Filtering on the primary key works.

presets.label: Generated columns (new in 18)
presets.lookFor: With `publish_generated_columns = stored` the stored `price_with_vat` is sent; the **virtual** `label` never is, because it has no stored value. Listing a stored generated column in a column list publishes it even with the default `none`. On the subscriber the target column must be an ordinary column.

presets.label: DDL is not replicated
presets.lookFor: The new column joins publications without a column list automatically, but the ALTER itself is not sent: the subscriber must add `coupon` first, or apply errors start.

presets.label: The WAL is the source
presets.lookFor: Logical decoding reads the same WAL as everything else; `pg_logical_emit_message` writes a record decoders pass through. Creating a logical slot needs `wal_level = logical`, which this playground runs without (it reports `replica`).

production.title: Upgrading a major version with near-zero downtime
production.problem: Physical replication cannot cross major versions, and a dump and restore of 2 TB takes many hours of read-only time.
production.outcome: The write freeze lasts as long as the final catch-up and the sequence sync, typically seconds to minutes instead of hours. Tables without a primary key were given one (or `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`) beforehand, because their UPDATEs would otherwise fail on the publisher.

pitfalls.title: UPDATE fails: "does not have a replica identity"
pitfalls.fix: Add a primary key, or `REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX` on a unique non-null index, or as a last resort `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`.

pitfalls.title: Replication stops on a conflict
pitfalls.fix: Fix the local data, or skip the remote transaction with `ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... SKIP (lsn = ...)` using the finish LSN from the log (with the default `streaming = parallel` it can be missing; set streaming to `on` and let the error repeat). Skipping drops the whole transaction. In 18, per-type conflict counters show what keeps happening; the `*_origin_differs` ones need `track_commit_timestamp = on` on the subscriber.

pitfalls.title: A dropped subscription leaves its slot behind
pitfalls.fix: Check `pg_replication_slots` on the publisher and drop orphaned slots; cap retention with `max_slot_wal_keep_size`.

pitfalls.title: Sequences and DDL silently drift
pitfalls.fix: Apply schema changes to the subscriber first (additive changes), and run `setval` for every sequence before a switchover.

pitfalls.title: Publishing a generated column into a generated column
pitfalls.fix: Either leave the option at `none` and let the subscriber compute the column itself, or make the subscriber column an ordinary column. Virtual generated columns are never published.

keyPointers: **Publication** (what to send) on the publisher, **subscription** (where from) on the subscriber, one logical **slot** per subscription.
Decoding is in **commit order**; rolled-back transactions are **never sent**.
**Replica identity** (default: primary key) identifies old rows; without one, published UPDATE/DELETE fail on the publisher.
**Row filters** turn UPDATEs into INSERT/DELETE when rows cross the filter; **column lists** limit columns but are not security.
Not replicated: **DDL, sequences, large objects**. Initial data is copied by table-sync workers, then changes stream.

lessons.title: Declarative partitioning and pruning
lessons.tldr: A **partitioned table** has no storage of its own: each row is routed by its partition key to one partition, an ordinary table with its own heap, indexes and statistics. Queries that constrain the key touch only the relevant partitions through **partition pruning**, and old data leaves by dropping a whole partition instead of deleting rows.

visualizer.title: Which partitions does a query touch?
visualizer.interaction: Pick a query and see where pruning happens (plan time, executor start, or run time), next to its EXPLAIN output. Then route a few rows and compare DELETE with DROP for retention.

presets.label: Partitions and routing
presets.lookFor: The parent stores nothing (0 bytes). `tableoid` shows which partition each row was routed to.

presets.label: Plan-time pruning
presets.lookFor: With pruning only `events_2026_10` appears. Turn it off and the plan becomes an Append over all five partitions.

presets.label: Pruning at executor start
presets.lookFor: Look for **Subplans Removed: 4**: the generic plan kept every partition, and pruning ran when the parameter became known.

presets.label: Pruning during execution
presets.lookFor: Four subplans say **(never executed)**: the value came from an InitPlan, so the Append pruned at run time.

presets.label: Unique keys must include the partition key
presets.lookFor: Each partition enforces uniqueness only inside itself, so a primary key on `id` alone is rejected. With `created_at` added it works, and the parent's key creates one index per partition.

presets.label: Retention: DELETE vs DROP
presets.lookFor: DELETE logged every row (about 1.2 MB) and left 22,320 dead rows for VACUUM. DROP removed a month in a few kB of WAL and left nothing to clean.

presets.label: Add next month with ATTACH
presets.lookFor: ATTACH takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE on the parent. The matching CHECK constraint lets it skip the validation scan; the DEFAULT partition is still checked for December rows.

presets.label: DEFAULT partition traps
presets.lookFor: A late row lands in the DEFAULT partition, and then creating January **fails**: the new bounds would make that row belong elsewhere. Moving the rows out and attaching in one transaction fixes it. As long as `partdefid` is set, `DETACH … CONCURRENTLY` is refused too.

production.title: Monthly partitions for a 3-year event log
production.problem: The monthly `DELETE` produced tens of GB of WAL, saturated the replica link, and left a month of dead rows that autovacuum took days to clear. Recent-data queries still walked indexes covering three years.
production.outcome: Retention became a metadata operation of a few kB of WAL (dropping a 22,000-row month writes about 6 kB, deleting it about 1.2 MB), with no dead rows. Recent-data queries touch one month instead of 36, so their indexes are 36 times smaller and stay in cache.

pitfalls.title: Queries that do not mention the partition key
pitfalls.fix: Partition by the column most queries filter on, add the key to hot queries, or accept the fan-out for rare queries.

pitfalls.title: DETACH CONCURRENTLY refused
pitfalls.fix: Avoid a DEFAULT partition on tables you rotate (create future partitions ahead of time instead), or use a plain DETACH in a short maintenance window.

pitfalls.title: Too many partitions
pitfalls.fix: Keep partition counts in the hundreds to low thousands, choose coarser ranges, and make sure common queries prune.

pitfalls.title: A DEFAULT partition that quietly fills up
pitfalls.fix: Create partitions ahead of time and alert when the default holds any rows. To add a range, move its rows out of the default and ATTACH in one transaction (the last playground preset).

keyPointers: RANGE / LIST / HASH; range bounds are **inclusive below, exclusive above**; the parent has **no storage**.
Pruning at **plan time** (constants), **executor start** (`Subplans Removed`), and **run time** (`(never executed)`).
PRIMARY KEY / UNIQUE must **include the partition key**; an index on the parent is created on every partition.
Retention: **DROP / DETACH a partition**, not DELETE; ATTACH with a matching CHECK to skip validation.
Autovacuum handles partitions, but **ANALYZE the parent** yourself.

lessons.title: Backups and point-in-time recovery
lessons.tldr: PostgreSQL backs up either **logically** with `pg_dump` (SQL or an archive of one database) or **physically** with a base backup of the whole cluster plus the continuous stream of archived WAL. Physical backups enable **point-in-time recovery**: restore the base backup and replay archived WAL up to any moment after it, such as one second before a destructive mistake.

visualizer.title: Recover to one minute before the mistake
visualizer.interaction: Step through a day with a base backup, archived WAL and a bad DROP, then recovery. Drag `recovery_target_time` to before 01:20, before 14:05, or after it and step again.

presets.label: What pg_dump does inside the server
presets.lookFor: A dump is one **REPEATABLE READ** transaction: every table is read in the same snapshot, so the output is consistent. It holds **AccessShareLock** on each table it dumps until the end, and no XID. `pg_export_snapshot()` is how `pg_dump -j` workers share that one snapshot.

presets.label: Archiving settings
presets.lookFor: This playground runs with archiving off. A PITR-ready server needs `wal_level` replica or higher, `archive_mode = on` and a working `archive_command` or `archive_library`.

presets.label: A low-level base backup
presets.lookFor: `labelfile` is the `backup_label` you must save with the copy: START WAL LOCATION and CHECKPOINT LOCATION tell recovery where to begin.

presets.label: Segment files and switches
presets.lookFor: `pg_switch_wal` closes the current segment so it can be archived now (what `archive_timeout` does on a timer). Every file is a full 16 MB.

presets.label: A named restore point
presets.lookFor: A `RESTORE_POINT` record sits in the WAL before the purge. Recovery could stop exactly there with `recovery_target_name = 'before_invoice_purge'`.

presets.label: Write the recovery settings
presets.lookFor: Targets can be a time, a restore point name, an LSN or an XID (one at a time). `pause` lets you check the data before ending recovery.

presets.label: Incremental backups need WAL summaries
presets.lookFor: `pg_basebackup --incremental` (17+) copies only blocks changed since a previous backup, using summaries written by the WAL summarizer. With `summarize_wal = off` there are none.

production.title: Undoing a bad migration with PITR
production.problem: A nightly `pg_dump` would restore last night's state and lose 13 hours of invoices. Restoring the base backup alone would do the same.
production.outcome: Data loss is bounded by the recovery target, one minute here, instead of 13 hours. Recovery time is dominated by replaying 13 hours of WAL; newer incremental backups (`pg_basebackup --incremental` + `pg_combinebackup`) or a more recent base backup shorten it.

pitfalls.title: An archive_command that lies
pitfalls.fix: Return 0 only after the file is durably stored, refuse to overwrite existing files, and test restores regularly. `pg_stat_archiver.failed_count` must stay flat.

pitfalls.title: Archiving silently stopped and pg_wal filled
pitfalls.fix: Alert on `failed_count` and on `pg_wal` size; fix the archive target. Never delete files from `pg_wal` by hand.

pitfalls.title: Treating pg_dump as the only backup
pitfalls.fix: Use base backups plus WAL archiving for recovery, and keep `pg_dump` for migrations, partial restores and cross-version moves. Verify base backups with `pg_verifybackup`.

pitfalls.title: pg_restore refuses the dump file
pitfalls.fix: Dump with `-Fc` or `-Fd` for anything you may restore selectively. Repeat `-t` / `-n` once per object (they do not take comma lists), use `-O` (`--no-owner`) when roles differ, and dump roles and tablespaces separately with `pg_dumpall --globals-only`, because `pg_dump` never includes them.

pitfalls.title: A long pg_dump blocks a migration and VACUUM
pitfalls.fix: Schedule DDL outside dump windows and set `lock_timeout` on migrations. Take large dumps from a standby, or rely on base backups and use `pg_dump` for smaller, targeted exports.

keyPointers: **pg_dump**: one database in one snapshot; plain SQL goes to **psql**, custom/directory archives to **pg_restore** (`-j`, `-L`); roles need **pg_dumpall --globals-only**.
**Base backup + archived WAL** = PITR; replay must start at the backup's `START WAL LOCATION`.
`restore_command` + `recovery.signal` + one **recovery_target_*** (time, name, lsn, xid, immediate).
Ending recovery starts a **new timeline**; `.history` files record branch points.
Incremental backups (17+) need **`summarize_wal`** and are rebuilt with **`pg_combinebackup`**.

lessons.title: Connection pooling
lessons.tldr: Every PostgreSQL connection is a separate backend process with its own memory and session state, so thousands of mostly idle connections waste RAM and slots up to `max_connections`. A **pooler** such as PgBouncer lets many clients share a few server connections, and its pooling mode decides which session features, such as `SET`, prepared statements, advisory locks and `LISTEN`, still behave correctly.

visualizer.title: Four clients, two server connections
visualizer.interaction: Step through the same client script in **transaction**, **session** and **statement** mode and watch where session state lands and what breaks.

presets.label: Session state a pooler can leak
presets.lookFor: All five live in **this backend**, not in the client. Under transaction pooling the next client on this server connection would inherit them, including the tenant_a search_path.

presets.label: DISCARD ALL wipes it
presets.lookFor: `DISCARD ALL` resets settings to their defaults, drops prepared statements and temp tables, releases session advisory locks and stops listening: every count is back to 0. Session-mode poolers run it between clients.

presets.label: Transaction-scoped alternatives
presets.lookFor: `SET LOCAL` and `pg_advisory_xact_lock` end with the transaction, so nothing survives COMMIT. This is what is safe under transaction pooling.

presets.label: Per-request context: set_config(…, true)
presets.lookFor: The third argument `true` makes the value transaction-local, like `SET LOCAL`, so a tenant id used by row-level security policies cannot leak to the next client on the connection. Afterwards the value is an **empty string**, not NULL. Without `missing_ok = true`, reading a name that was never set raises an error.

presets.label: What one connection costs
presets.lookFor: Even this idle backend holds about 2 MB in memory contexts (caches, plans), before any query runs, and each query can add `work_mem` per sort or hash node. The playground has one standalone backend; a server forks one process per connection.

presets.label: Timeouts that protect a pool
presets.lookFor: All are off (0) by default. `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` kills sessions that sit in an open transaction holding locks and an old snapshot; `idle_session_timeout` is dangerous behind a pooler, which keeps idle server connections on purpose.

presets.label: Idle in transaction holds an XID
presets.lookFor: While a transaction stays open its `backend_xid` and snapshot hold back VACUUM cluster-wide. A pooled client that forgets COMMIT pins a server connection and the cleanup horizon.

presets.label: Find the sessions that hog the pool
presets.lookFor: On a server, sort `idle in transaction` sessions by `xact_open_for` to find the ones holding connections and snapshots. `pg_terminate_backend(pid)` returns true once the signal is **sent**; with a `timeout` in ms it returns true only if the backend actually exited.

production.title: From 4,000 connections to 60
production.problem: The server needed `max_connections = 5000`; each backend kept its own caches and memory even when idle, connection storms during deploys forked hundreds of processes at once, and snapshot work grows with the number of backends.
production.outcome: The primary serves the same traffic with about 60 busy backends instead of 4,000 mostly idle ones, deploys no longer cause fork storms, and memory goes to `shared_buffers` and `work_mem` instead of idle processes. A sensible pool size is a small multiple of CPU cores, measured under load.

pitfalls.title: Session SET under transaction pooling
pitfalls.fix: Use `SET LOCAL` inside a transaction, or pass settings per role/database (`ALTER ROLE … SET`). Schema-qualify names instead of relying on `search_path`.

pitfalls.title: Session advisory locks that never unlock
pitfalls.fix: Use `pg_advisory_xact_lock` (released at COMMIT) or route lock holders through a session-mode pool.

pitfalls.title: Prepared statements "do not exist"
pitfalls.fix: Enable the pooler's prepared-statement support (PgBouncer 1.21+ `max_prepared_statements`) for protocol-level statements, or disable server-side prepares in the driver. SQL-level `PREPARE` is never safe in transaction mode.

pitfalls.title: A new connection for every query
pitfalls.fix: Create one pool per application process (the driver's built-in pool or a pool library) and borrow from it per request; add a server-side pooler when many processes connect.

pitfalls.title: Drivers that leave transactions open
pitfalls.fix: Use autocommit for read paths, always end transactions (commit or rollback in a `finally`), and set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` as a backstop.

keyPointers: One connection = **one backend process** with private memory; `max_connections` (100) sizes shared memory and slots.
**Session** mode: safe but no multiplexing. **Transaction** mode: multiplexes, breaks session state. **Statement** mode: autocommit only.
Session state lives in the backend: **SET, PREPARE, session advisory locks, LISTEN, temp tables**; `DISCARD ALL` resets it.
Transaction-safe forms: **`SET LOCAL`**, **`pg_advisory_xact_lock`**, schema-qualified names.
Guard the pool with **`idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`**; avoid `idle_session_timeout` behind a pooler.
